However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Gen Zers are apt to try cold-weather challenges like “winter arc.” But they’re also the generation most likely to say they generally quit challenges before finishing and set the same money goal more than once due to not sticking with it.

It’s not technically winter yet, but depending on where you live, it may feel like it. For many of us, this is a time of hibernation, but for others, it’s prime time for a glow-up.

“Winter arc” is a popular social media challenge through which people aim to improve themselves before the new year. It typically runs from October through December, but can be started any time during the cold months. The aim is to jump-start the “new year, new me” season before the ball even drops.

Whether they call it a winter arc or not, plenty of Americans are working on self-improvement as the chill sets in. According to a new NerdWallet survey, conducted online by The Harris Poll, 75% of Americans say they’re working on their physical health, and 69% say the same about their finances.

Popular as it is, winter arc isn’t the only cold-weather challenge out there. The survey found that half of Americans (50%) say they’ve tried some sort of winter improvement challenge. And no one likes a challenge like Gen Z: Nearly three-quarters of Gen Zers (74%) have tried a winter challenge, compared with 64% of millennials, 42% of Gen Xers and 29% of baby boomers.

Note: The survey defines Gen Zers as those 18-29; millennials, ages 30-45; Gen Xers, ages 46-61 and baby boomers, ages 62-80.

But there’s a difference between starting a challenge and successfully completing one. Gen Zers reign supreme as those most likely to hop on a winter challenge. But they’re also the most likely to say they generally quit challenges before finishing, buy products they saw on social media in an effort to stick with the challenges and set the same financial goal more than once.

Gen Zers are more likely than any other generation to say they:

Have tried a winter financial challenge other than no-spend January (21%, vs. 11% of millennials, 5% of Gen Xers and 2% of baby boomers).

Generally quit challenges before they finish them (59%, vs. 42% of millennials, 36% of Gen Xers and 22% of baby boomers).

Expect to spend more on at least one discretionary expense this winter than they would during another season (90%, vs. 83% of millennials, 61% of Gen Xers and 48% of baby boomers).

Put off dealing with money until after the holidays (60%, vs. 47% of millennials, 35% of Gen Xers and 15% of baby boomers).

Aren’t currently working on improving their finances, but want to make it a priority (15%, vs. 8% of millennials and 6% each of Gen Xers and baby boomers).

“Embracing the winter arc trend can be a great way to find motivation to make progress on a goal over the slower winter months,” says Kimberly Palmer, personal finance expert at NerdWallet. “Pick a winter challenge that aligns with a longer-term goal for the coming year.”

Winter challenges popular with Gen Z include diet- or fitness-related challenges (29%) and self-improvement challenges, like winter arc or 75 Hard, a mental toughness challenge that runs for 75 days and includes two workouts every day, a strict diet and daily nonfiction reading (25%).

While winter arcs typically focus on physical, mental and intellectual self-improvement, Gen Z is game to try a financial challenge as well: One long-standing financial challenge — no-spend January — is more popular among younger Americans (22% of Gen Zers and 20% of millennials) than their older counterparts (12% of Gen Xers and 6% of baby boomers). As for other types of financial challenges, Gen Z is more likely than any other generation to have tried at least one: 21% compared with 11% of millennials, 5% of Gen X and 2% of baby boomers.

Of course, it’s one thing to try a challenge, during wintertime or otherwise. It’s another thing entirely to follow through and complete it. That’s the hard part for many Gen Zers.

When taking on a self-improvement challenge, the beginning tends to be easiest. You’re motivated and excited to reach goals and better yourself. But as time goes on, it’s easy to slip back into old habits or for the shine of a brand-new challenge to dim. And Gen Zers report that they are most likely to quit early.

According to the survey, nearly 3 in 5 Gen Zers (59%) say they generally quit challenges before they finish them. That compares with 42% of millennials, 36% of Gen Xers and 22% of baby boomers.

Along with challenges in general, money goals can be difficult to follow through with, especially for younger Americans. Around two-thirds of Gen Zers (64%) say it’s been hard to stick to financial goals they’ve set in the past, compared with 52% of Gen Xers and 34% of baby boomers. Gen Zers are more likely than any other generation to say they’ve set the same financial goal more than once because they didn’t stick with it — 33%, compared with 20% of millennials, 15% of Gen Xers and 7% of baby boomers.

This isn’t for lack of desire, though. Seven in 10 Gen Zers (70%) say they’re working on improving their finances. All generations show high levels of effort here: 76% each of millennials and Gen Xers say the same, along with 59% of baby boomers.

So why is it so hard to stick with money goals? One possibility is that it’s difficult to see meaningful progress on finances, particularly when you’re young. According to the survey, 65% of Gen Zers say it’s harder to see progress on financial goals than on physical goals.

This makes perfect sense for this age group — for those light on money but rich in youthfulness, desired physical changes may show up faster than financial progress. On top of that, the current job market is tough for younger Americans. Recent college grads now have a higher unemployment rate than workers in general. Even if you’re still on the job hunt, your 20s are a great time to start taking steps, however small, toward building future wealth.» MORE: I’m 25. Here’s How I Got Started Investing

“To increase your chances of success, try coordinating winter arc plans with a friend or giving yourself smaller goals along the way,” Palmer says. “Leaning on the support or coaching from a loved one can make it easier to keep going, as can celebrating incremental progress.”

Self-improvement is a noble pursuit. But as with most things in life, it’s easy to lose sight of the ultimate goal in favor of buying things to help you reach it.

“It’s easy to feel like a quick purchase can help us meet our goals, and sometimes a product can be a useful tool, but the reality is that true winter arc progress comes from putting in the hard work. There’s no option for ‘purchasing’ it instead,” Palmer says.

According to the survey, more than a quarter of Gen Zers (26%) say they’ve bought a product they saw on social media to help with a personal goal or challenge. This is more than any other generation: 17% of millennials, 11% of Gen Xers and 7% of baby boomers say they’ve made social media buys for self-betterment.

Some self-improvement purchases may be billed on a monthly basis. More than 1 in 5 Gen Zers (23%) say they're still paying for a subscription or membership they signed up for during a past goal or challenge. This is also true for 17% of millennials, 9% of Gen Xers and 2% of baby boomers.

These challenge purchases may pile onto already higher winter expenses. A majority of Gen Zers (90%) say they expect to spend more on at least one discretionary expense this winter than they would during another season, more than any other generation. Top expenses include food delivery (38%), entertainment at home (35%) and indoor family entertainment (30%). A quarter of Gen Zers (25%) expect to spend more on fitness or wellness apps this winter compared to other seasons.

Some may be spending more to make themselves feel better during the cold, gray months. Nearly 1 in 5 Gen Zers (18%) say they tend to combat winter blues by spending money, compared with 10% of Gen Xers and 3% of baby boomers.

The holiday season is an expensive time of year for many of us, and it’s easy to sweep finances under the rug until the new year. According to the survey, 3 in 5 Gen Zers (60%) say they generally put off dealing with money until after the holidays. This is more than any other generation: 47% of millennials, 35% of Gen Xers and 15% of baby boomers say the same.

Even for those taking on financial challenges before the new year hits, it’s easy for the resulting “savings” to disappear. Nearly three-quarters of Gen Zers (74%) say money they save by cutting back in one area usually just gets spent somewhere else instead of staying “saved.” This is also true for 68% of millennials, 63% of Gen Xers and 45% of baby boomers.

For some, the holidays are just one thing competing for their money. Over half of Gen Zers (52%) say they’d rather spend money on how they look now than save it for their future financial security. This compares with 26% of Gen Xers and 13% of baby boomers.

We don’t begrudge anyone for their desire to look and feel their best this upcoming season. But that doesn’t have to mean you can’t level up your money at the same time.

More than 2 in 5 Gen Zers (43%) say they’re putting consistent work into improving their finances, and 27% are putting some work into this, but not consistently. Moreover, 15% of Gen Zers aren’t working on improving their finances but want to make them a priority. No matter your age, here are some ideas for a financial glow-up before the spring thaw.

Start small if you tend to quit. Nearly 2 in 5 Americans (38%) say they generally quit challenges before finishing them. Early-challenge motivation can make it easy to overcommit. If you often take on challenges impulsively then peter out a few weeks later, try starting small. For example, maybe no-spend January is a stretch, but you can still save by intentionally creating two no-spend days a week.

Move money the day you save it. Over 3 in 5 Americans (61%) say money they save by cutting back in one area usually gets spent somewhere else. If you’re cutting back, transfer the difference to savings that same day, so it can’t leak out elsewhere.

Make money progress measurable. Half of Americans (50%) say it’s harder to see progress on financial goals than physical goals. There’s a saying that what gets measured, gets managed. Choose one number to track. This might be down payment savings, debt payoff progress or an investment milestone. It may not move much month to month, but you’d be surprised at the difference a year can make, even without a ton of money each month to dedicate toward your goal.

Begin before January. More than a third of Americans (37%) say they put off dealing with money until after the holidays. Facing your finances during the often busy and expensive final months of the year can be daunting, but don’t put your head in the sand until after the holiday credit card balances come due. Put a cap on your winter spending before the new year to avoid going overboard during the tempting sales this time of year.

“If you’re trying to choose a winter arc, pick one that’s realistic but also a stretch goal, so it’s satisfying to accomplish while not being completely out of reach,” Palmer suggests. “Chances are you’ll be glad with what you got done over the colder months when springtime hits.”

#2967. Viking: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Goodwill vouchers and a 60% rebooking rate suggest river guests stayed loyal through a costly disruption, a test many cruise operators have yet to face.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings conference call, held on Nov. 17, 2026, Viking (VIK +4.43%) reported total revenue of $2.2 billion, an increase of 9.2% year-over-year. The company's fleet diversification into ocean cruising and its guest retention efforts help cushion earnings against seasonal disruptions in river cruising. Three key takeaways from management explain where the business is headed next.

Unprecedented low water levels across European rivers reduced third-quarter revenue and adjusted gross margin, defined as total revenue minus direct variable costs, by $100 million each. Management issued goodwill vouchers to preserve guest trust, and 60% of rebooked guests selected 2027 river itineraries.

Viking is expanding its presence in ocean cruises, where it holds a 27% market share in the luxury category. Revenue per passenger cruise day, which measures daily guest ticket revenue, increased in the ocean segment as advance bookings for 2026 rose 17% year over year.

The company ended the quarter with $4.1 billion in cash and cash equivalents while maintaining net leverage, calculated as net debt divided by adjusted earnings, at 1.2 times. Management deployed $350 million to repurchase shares under its $1.0 billion authorization while securing options for 10 additional river vessels.

Advance bookings across core products reached 68% of 2027 capacity by early November, proving that consumer demand isn't waning despite temporary weather impacts. Fleet expansion options, strong brand equity, and high repeat customer rates provide structural protection while management maintains pricing discipline.

Viking continues to balance fleet expansion across river and ocean segments with a conservative balance sheet.

TL;DR: Mortgage rates continue to climb under pressure from inflation.

Mortgage rates keep rising as markets anticipate a near-certain Fed rate hike next month.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage rose to 7.34% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is seven basis points higher than yesterday and 34 basis points higher than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

On Friday, the Bureau of Labor Statistics released the Producer Price Index for October, which tracks the change in prices that U.S. producers are able to get for their products. This is one way to measure inflation on the market end, rather than the consumer end.

The results were mixed. While prices didn’t rise quite as high as economists anticipated month-over-month (0.3% vs. 0.4%), year-over-year price growth did reach 6.5% — the largest increase in four years. This points to even higher costs for consumers coming in the near future.

Investors are convinced that the Federal Reserve will raise overnight borrowing rates again in December to pull inflation down. And higher overnight borrowing rates — called the federal funds rate, which is what banks pay to fund products like mortgages — usually lead to higher mortgage rates.

» MORE: How the Federal Reserve affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.84% or higher.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

» Stay informed: Check out NerdWallet's mortgage news hub for all our latest coverage.

The rate you see advertised is a sample rate — usually for a borrower with perfect credit, making a big down payment, and paying for mortgage points. That won't match every buyer's circumstances.

In addition to market factors outside of your control, your customized quote depends on your:

Even two people with similar credit scores might get different rates, depending on their overall financial profiles.

#2961. Euroseas (ESEA) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Management weighs fleet growth against rising newbuild deliveries ahead.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Euroseas (ESEA -4.65%) reported a decrease in quarterly revenue due to a reduction in its operational fleet size while maintaining high utilization across its vessels. Management reported that the company is executing a fleet expansion strategy with 12 newbuilding vessels on order, which is expected to increase total capacity to 95,000 TEU by 2029. The company indicated that its chartering coverage for 2027 remains at 90%, providing cash flow visibility despite projected market volatility. Management stated that the current valuation of the company's shares reflects a significant discount to its estimated net asset value.

Operator: Thank you for standing by, ladies and gentlemen, and welcome to the Euroseas conference call on the third quarter 2026 financial results. We have with us Mr. Aristides Pittas, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer; and Mr. Tasos Aslidis, Chief Financial Officer of the company. [Operator Instructions] I must advise you that this conference is being recorded today. Please be reminded that the company announced their results with a press release that has been publicly distributed. Before passing the floor over to Mr. Pittas, I would like to remind everyone that in today's presentation and conference call, Euroseas will be making forward-looking statements. These statements are within the meaning of the federal securities laws.

Matters discussed may be forward-looking statements, which are based on current management expectations that involve risks and uncertainties that may result in such expectations not being realized. I kindly draw your attention to Slide #2 of the webcast presentation, which has the full forward-looking statement, and the same statement was also included in the press release. Please take a moment to go through the whole statement and read it. And now, I would like to turn the floor over to Mr. Pittas. Thank you, sir. Please go ahead.

Aristides Pittas: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen, and thank you all for joining us today for our scheduled conference call. Together [Audio Gap] Tasos Aslidis, our Chief Financial Officer. The purpose of today's call is to discuss our financial results for the 3- and 9-month period ended September 30, 2026. Please turn to Slide 3 of the presentation for our quarterly financial highlights. For the third quarter of 2026, we reported total net revenues of $54.07 million and a net income attributable to controlling shareholders of $25.64 million or $3.65 per diluted share. Adjusted net income attributable to common shareholders for the quarter was $30.7 million or 4.37 -- or $4.37 per diluted share. Adjusted EBITDA for the period was $38.29 million.

Please refer to the press release for the reconciliation between net income and adjusted net income and net income to adjusted EBITDA. Our CFO, Tasos Aslidis, will go over the financial highlights in more detail later on. Reflecting our continued commitment to delivering value to shareholders, our Board of Directors has declared an increased quarterly common stock dividend of $0.85 per share for the third quarter of 2026, compared to $0.80 per share in the previous quarter. This represents a 6.25% sequential increase and a 21.4% increase year-over-year, reflecting our confidence in the company's financial strength and cash flow generation.

The dividend will be payable on or about December 16 to shareholders of record as of December 9, 2026 under the company's common stock dividend plan. Based on current share price levels, the distribution reflects an annualized yield of approximately 5.2%. Since the launch of our $20 million share repurchase program in May 2022, we have repurchased 480,000 shares in the open market through November 17, 2026, representing approximately 6.8% of our outstanding shares for a total consideration of around $11.4 million. The plan has been renewed until July 2020 -- 2027. We remain committed to executing the program in a disciplined and opportunistic manner, allocating capital prudently while enhancing long-term value for our shareholders.

Please turn to Slide 4 for an overview of our recent developments, covering key activities across vessel sales and acquisitions, chartering and fleet operations. On the S&P front, as previously announced, the company sold Motor Vessel Evridiki G, a 2,556 TEU vessel built in 2001, for $26 million. The vessel has been delivered to her new owners, an unaffiliated third party, on October 31, 2026. We expect to record a gain from the sale of approximately $22.5 million, which will be accounted for in our Q4 results. The sale reflects our strategic move to gradually renew our fleet and maximize returns for our shareholders in the longer run.

On the chartering side, we extended the time charter of Motor Vessel Jonathan P for a minimum of 24 to 26 months at $26,000 per day and fixed Motor Vessel EM Corfu for 12 to 14 months at $62,500 per day. The new EM Corfu charter is expected to start in mid-December following the completion of her scheduled drydocking. In addition, the charterer has exercised its 5-year options on our 4 newbuilds, Motor Vessel Elena, Motor Vessel Nikitas G, Motor Vessel Thrylos and Motor Vessel Socrates Ch, which we will take delivery of between mid-2027 and mid-2028, at $32,500 per day per vessel, further enhancing our earnings visibility.

On the operational side, Motor Vessel Evridiki G incurred 69 days of planned off-hire due to its scheduled drydocking between July 1 and September 7, 2026. Otherwise, we recorded no commercial off-hire during the quarter. Please turn to Slide 5. Our operating fleet currently consists of 20 vessels with a combined carrying capacity of about 59,000 TEU and a TEU-weighted average age of 12.5 years. The fleet comprises 6 intermediate containerships with a combined carrying capacity of approximately 25,000 TEU and an average age of around 18 years, alongside 14 feeder containerships with a [Technical Difficulty] capacity of approximately 33,000 TEU and an average age of around 8 years.

We have 12 newbuilding vessels on order, comprising 8 feeder and 4 intermediate containerships, with deliveries scheduled from the third quarter of 2027 through the first quarter of 2029. Upon completion of our newbuilding program, our fleet will expand to 32 vessels and a total carrying capacity of approximately 95,000 TEU. Please turn to Slide 6 for a further update on our fleet employment and forward coverage. Our chartering coverage stands at 100% for 2026, 90% for 2027 and almost 50% for 2028 at attractive average daily rates of approximately $30,000, $32,500 and $31,000 respectively. Even if all our open days in 2028 earned zero charter, the year would still be profitable as well.

Moving on to Slide 8, let's walk through the key market developments that shaped the containership sector during the third quarter. The containership market firmed further through the third quarter, helped by resilient demand after the peak season and logistical bottlenecks down the whole supply chain. Charter rates have climbed again in recent weeks, with current rates for feeder to post-Panamax tonnage well above third quarter averages as liners continue to compete for scarce ships. Freight rates have also held firm, rising further in October.

On the asset side, secondhand prices rose about 2.5% over the quarter and remain near the highest levels since mid-2022, while newbuilding prices held steady at elevated levels, reflecting strong yard demand and high construction costs. Idle capacity, excluding vessels under repair, was just 250,000 TEU, or 0.7% of the global fleet, as of early November. This is a historic low and confirms the structural tightness in the cycle. Recycling has also remained totally subdued, with only 11 vessels totaling 27,000 TEU sent to scrap year-to-date, reflecting again how valuable tonnage remains. Scrap prices have recently increased to about $530 per lightweight ton. Meanwhile, the global fleet has already grown by 4.2% year-to-date.

Please turn to Slide 9, which illustrates the development of 6- to 12-month time charter rates over the past decade. Across the board, from the smaller feeders through to the larger intermediate container segments, current charter rates remain well above both their 10-year median and average levels. Across the 4 size segments shown, today's rates are roughly 65% to 80% higher than the 10-year averages. These vessel classes remain essential to maintaining network flexibility and supporting regional and intra-regional trade flows, a role that has only grown in importance amid the ongoing geopolitical uncertainty and supply chain realignment. Please turn to Slide 10, where we review the global macroeconomic backdrop and its implications for container shipping demand.

According to the IMF's October 2026 World Economic Outlook, global economic activity has remained resilient despite ongoing geopolitical disruptions and elevated energy prices and trade uncertainty. Global GDP growth is projected at 3.1% in 2026, but recovering to 3.4% in 2027. The resilience has been supported by continued investment in artificial intelligence, technology-related demand and the ability of economies to adapt to geopolitical and trade disruptions. However, performance remains uneven. Technology-linked economies and energy exporters are holding up better, while energy importers outside the technology supply chain face a tougher outlook.

Meanwhile, inflationary pressures remain elevated, with global headline inflation projected to rise to 4.7% by the end of 2026, largely on higher energy prices, before easing to 4.1% in 2027. Risks remain tilted to the downside, particularly from further geopolitical escalation, renewed trade tensions, fiscal vulnerabilities and the potential reassessment of AI-related investment expectations. Turning to the major economies, U.S. growth is projected to remain steady at 2.3% in both 2026 and 2027. The IMF has revised China's growth forecast slightly lower, down by 0.1 percentage points to 4.5%, noting that resilient exports are no longer sufficient to fully offset persistent weakness in domestic demand. Growth is expected by the IMF to moderate further to 4% in 2027.

In the ASEAN-5 economies, growth is projected at 4.4% in 2026 and 4.3% in 2027, putting the region ahead of China in 2027 for the first time. Looking at global trade, world trade volume growth is slightly moderating in 2026 compared to 2025 whilst remaining quite strong at 4.2%, and it will stabilize there in 2027. Importantly, however, for our sector, Clarksons expects TEU-miles to turn slightly negative in 2027 and grow by just 1% in 2028 due to the normalization of the trade routes they expect to see within the next 24 months. Turning on to Slide 11, you can see the total fleet age profile and containership outlook.

The overall containership fleet remains relatively young, with a majority of vessels under 15 years of age and only about 15% of the fleet over 20 years old. However, this aggregate view is totally different when examining the feeder and intermediate segments in isolation. Turning to vessel deliveries, the top right chart illustrates scheduled new deliveries as a percentage of the existing fleet. Deliveries are projected at approximately 5.5% for 2026, 9.9% for 2027 and just under 30% for 2028 onwards, although actual fleet growth is expected to be somewhat lower due to slippage and future demolition activity. The bottom chart places the current order book in historical context.

At approximately 44.4% of the existing fleet as of November 2026, the order book stands at its highest level in more than 15 years, which warrants close attention as we assess the medium-term supply outlook for the sector. The overall containership order book is now up about 26% since the start of 2026. Turning to Slide 12, we highlight the age profile and order book for the 1,000 to 3,000 TEU feeder segment. The supply picture here is very different from the broader market, starting with a striking age profile difference.

Approximately 23% of the fleet is between 15 and 19 years old, and 31% is over 20 years old, meaning more than half of the feeder fleet is approaching scrapping age. As environmental regulations tighten and compliance costs rise, a meaningful portion of these older vessels will likely exit the market over the coming years, depending on how challenging market conditions become. Against this aging backdrop, newbuilding activity in the sub-3,000 TEU segment remains very limited at below 20% of the existing fleet, well below the 44.4% for the global containership fleet, pointing to a more favorable supply outlook for smaller vessels.

Scheduled deliveries represent just 3.2% of the existing fleet in 2026, 8.5% in 2027 and 9.4% in 2028 and beyond. Let's move to Slide 13 to focus on the intermediate segment, the other core segment of our fleet. As of November 2026, the order book in this segment stands at approximately 31% of the existing fleet. Whilst that is higher than in the feeder segment, it remains modest relative to the larger mainline vessel classes, where newbuilding activity has been considerably more pronounced. What makes this segment particularly compelling from a supply perspective is the age profile.

Approximately 32% of the vessels in this size range are over 20 years old, with a further 34% between 15 and 19 years old. This means roughly 2/3 of the fleet is approaching the age where retirement becomes likely, especially as environmental compliance requirements grow more stringent and costly, as we have noted before. Scheduled deliveries are predicted at 4% of the fleet in 2026, rising to 8.3% in 2027 and around 20% in 2028 and beyond. When weighed against the potential for accelerated scrapping among the older segments, net fleet growth in the segment is expected to remain contained over the coming years.

The interplay between a maturing fleet and a measured newbuilding pipeline continues to underpin a structurally supportive environment for intermediate containership operators. Moving on to Slide 14, which sets what we have just discussed against the containership sector as a whole. The most striking feature is how heavily newbuilding activity is concentrated in the larger sectors. Order books in the neo-Panamax and post-Panamax segments range from approximately 36% to 112% of their existing fleet, as capacity is added for the main lane routes between major hubs. These are the vessel classes where oversupply concerns are most acute. At the same time, though, regional distribution relies on feeders, so more main lane volume increases the need for them as well.

With a significant portion of the fleet approaching replacement age, net fleet growth in these segments is likely to remain constrained and capacity could even shrink, while the larger classes and the overall fleet continue to expand. This underpins our conviction that Euroseas' fleet is positioned in segments with a supportive supply outlook and limited risk of oversupply. Please turn to Slide 15, where we summarize our outlook on the container sector. As we already discussed, the container market stayed strong through the third quarter of 2026 and continues to improve due to resilient trade growth, market disruptions and the lack of available tonnage.

Looking ahead to 2027, however, the outlook becomes more challenging, as a record wave of newbuilding deliveries and a possible return to normal Red Sea routing could weaken the supply-demand balance. Importantly, regardless of when traffic returns to Suez, our modeling indicates that fundamentals could deteriorate significantly from the second half of 2027 onwards, as the delivery schedule accelerates and fleet growth outpaces trade growth. Geopolitical uncertainty, however, could still alter this picture. Our modeling suggests the imbalance could widen further in 2028, adding to the pressure on freight and charter rates. But again, geopolitics, inefficiencies and logistical supply constraints may keep the market higher than fundamentals alone would suggest. Please turn now to Slide 16.

The left chart traces the 1-year time charter rate for 2,500 TEU containerships over the past decade. As of November 13, the 1-year rate for a 2,500 TEU vessel stands at $42,000 per day, well above the 10-year average of $25,000 per day and the median of $17,500. This strength, of course, is also reflected in asset values. The right chart shows newbuilding prices of $46 million, compared with a 10-year median of $40 million and an average of $37 million, while a 10-year-old vessel is valued at $44 million, more than double its 10-year median of $20 million and well above its average of $23.5 million.

These elevated secondhand valuations, particularly without attached employment, offer a less attractive risk-reward profile at this stage of the cycle. Newbuildings, by contrast, offer greater pricing flexibility and cost predictability. This conviction has driven our decision to expand our order book to the 12 vessels, building on the 9 vessels we completed in early 2025. This strategy, combined with our strong balance sheet and substantial liquidity, leaves us well-capitalized to pursue accretive opportunities as they arise, while our fleet's lower operating costs and environmental advantages set us apart competitively. #2956. Klarna: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Card users shop about three times as often, so every point of card adoption compounds into purchase frequency for shareholders.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 17, 2026, Klarna (KLAR +4.70%) reported that total revenue rose 12% year over year to $1.09 billion. The payment provider is shifting its long-term focus from acquiring new users to increasing average revenue per active consumer. Three key takeaways from management highlight how this strategic pivot is shaping up.

Fair Financing offers longer installment loans that generate higher profit margins per dollar spent than short-term payment options. Scaling these loan products in the U.S. and introducing them into European markets helps boost average customer revenue over time.

The company's payment card lets consumers choose between debit and interest-free installments at checkout. Card users make purchases roughly three times as frequently as non-card users, making card adoption a key driver of engagement.

The company offloads consumer loans through forward-flow programs, in which outside buyers commit to purchasing loans upfront. This setup allows the business to recycle capital into new lending while maintaining direct customer relationships.

Fourth-quarter transaction volume is accelerating toward 30% year-over-year growth in the U.S., supported by expanding payment card adoption and point-of-sale financing. Deep integrations with payment service providers (third-party distribution partners that connect payment software to online merchants) provide a steady source of low-cost merchant expansion.

Management is prioritizing deeper monetization over pure user acquisition, using high-margin subscription plans and flexible lending products to increase revenue per customer in established markets.

John Gibson: Well, I appreciate all of you being on the call. It was a good quarter. ROVs were busy. We got out and executed the work really well. We're not having execution issues. #2941. 2 of the Best Dividend Stocks to Buy With $5,000 in November

These two dividend stocks offer reliable raises year after year.

Investors with different goals and preferences will gravitate toward different companies, even if they have the same investment strategy. That's why it's so hard to come up with "the best" of any category of stocks. But we can still give it a try. Consider the following two companies: Johnson & Johnson (JNJ -1.36%) and Walmart (WMT -0.69%). Both are longtime market leaders with excellent dividend programs and are arguably among the top income stocks, given their impressive track records.

For those with $5,000 to spare (make sure it isn't set aside for emergencies), Johnson & Johnson and Walmart are two of the first dividend stocks I'd recommend buying this month. Here is why.

Johnson & Johnson has shown its resilience this year. Despite macroeconomic problems, a major U.S. patent cliff it experienced last year, and several of its medicines being targeted by government-led drug price negotiations, the healthcare giant has performed well. Third-quarter revenue increased by 5.9% year over year to $25.4 billion.

Johnson & Johnson's adjusted earnings per share declined 7.5% year over year to $2.59, primarily due to acquisition-related expenses. Overall, the business is healthy, and Johnson & Johnson once again increased its guidance for the full fiscal year 2026. The company now expects operational sales of $100.7 billion at the midpoint, representing a 6.9% year-over-year increase, versus midpoint sales and year-over-year growth of $100.6 billion and 6.8% year-over-year for its previous guidance.

Johnson & Johnson has also made meaningful clinical and regulatory progress this year, which should help the company boost sales and navigate patent cliffs over the medium term. In March, the company earned approval for Icotyde, a medicine for plaque psoriasis. It has had an impressive commercial ramp-up so far. As management noted, more than 20,000 patients have initiated treatment with Icotyde so far.

The company believes this drug can generate more than $5 billion in peak annual sales. And it boasts several other brand-new approvals or pipeline candidates that it believes can approach or even exceed the $5 billion annual sales milestone. We haven't even mentioned Johnson & Johnson's medtech business, where it has also made progress this year.

The company has earned clearance for the Ottava system, a robotic-assisted surgery device that will help it tap into an underpenetrated market. Johnson & Johnson looks unstoppable right now, and the company could continue delivering excellent returns for a while, especially once we factor in the dividend, which investors should seriously consider reinvesting.

Johnson & Johnson is a Dividend King, a company with a minimum of 50 consecutive annual dividend increases. Investors can get 17 shares of Johnson & Johnson with $5,000 right now. That'd be money well spent.

Walmart has also performed well this year, despite economic headwinds that have weighed on much of the retail industry. In the second quarter of its fiscal year 2027, which ended July 31, the company's revenue increased by 5.9% year over year to $187.9 billion. Adjusted EPS rose 19.1% year over year to $0.81. Importantly, membership revenue, e-commerce sales, and advertising revenue all grew much faster than retail sales.

These are three crucial, higher-margin businesses that should help lift the company's profits over the long run. Here's another important point to consider. While many legacy retailers went out of business -- or are currently struggling to stay in business -- because they failed to capitalize on the shift toward e-commerce, Walmart made no such mistake.

It currently stands as the second largest e-commerce player in the U.S. That highlights the company's ability to capitalize on new technologies, and it is doing the same with artificial intelligence (AI). Walmart is leveraging AI across much of its business, including in optimizing inventory management and improving supply chain efficiency. It is also using AI to personalize customers' shopping experiences, which can lead to higher sales volume.

Walmart's AI efforts could make a meaningful impact over the long run. Meanwhile, the company still has many of the same strengths that made it so successful. It is one of the largest retailers in the U.S., with a vast network of locations -- 90% of the U.S. population lives within 10 miles of one of the company's stores. Further, Walmart leverages its large retail footprint to negotiate attractive prices and discounts with wholesalers and passes those cost savings onto customers. The result: Walmart tends to offer lower prices for items.

These are important competitive advantages that could enable the company to perform well over the long run, while continuously raising its dividends. Walmart is also a Dividend King -- it has raised its payouts for 53 consecutive years. Investors can buy 38 shares of the company for $5,000 right now. For long-term dividend-seeking investors, that might be a great move.

#2938. Johnson & Johnson vs. Vertex Pharmaceuticals: Which Healthcare Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Johnson & Johnson's diversified MedTech and pharma mix faces off against Vertex's cystic fibrosis dominance, but their valuation gap tells a story worth weighing.

Healthcare investors often choose between established stability and high-growth innovation. Determining whether Johnson & Johnson (JNJ -1.36%) or Vertex Pharmaceuticals (VRTX -0.67%) is the superior choice requires examining their financial health and long-term strategies.

Johnson & Johnson is a diversified giant pivoting toward its most profitable medical technology and innovative medicine segments. Vertex Pharmaceuticals is a specialized biotechnology leader that is successfully diversifying its pipeline beyond its core treatments. Both companies provide unique advantages for investors looking toward 2027.

As a giant among healthcare stocks, the company focuses on its Innovative Medicine and MedTech segments to drive global growth. It distributes medications and devices to retailers, wholesalers, and hospitals, with a strategy centered on oncology, immunology, and neuroscience. Notable collaborations include an exclusive license for Darzalex from Genmab A/S (GMAB +0.76%) and a partnership with AbbVie (ABBV -0.59%) to co-commercialize the cancer drug Imbruvica.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 27, 2026, revenue reached about $99.3 billion, representing growth of roughly 7.8% compared to the prior period. During this same time frame, it reported net income of approximately $16.1 billion. This performance highlights the company's ability to maintain substantial revenue while navigating the complexities of the global medical marketplace.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the company maintains a debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 0.6x, which measures the balance between its total debt and shareholder equity. Its current ratio stands at nearly 1.0x, a metric that indicates whether a firm can cover its short-term obligations with its current assets. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 28, 2025, free cash flow was around $19.7 billion, providing ample capital for research and dividends.

Vertex Pharmaceuticals dominates the market for cystic fibrosis treatments and is aggressively expanding into gene-editing and acute pain therapies. It primarily sells its products to specialty pharmacies and distributors that provide access to patients and healthcare providers worldwide. The company is also collaborating with CRISPR Therapeutics (CRSP -0.55%) to develop innovative therapies for serious blood disorders.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached about $13.0 billion, which indicates a growth rate of roughly 10.5% over the previous twelve-month period. The company also reported net income of approximately $4.0 billion during this time. This steady growth reflects the strong demand for its specialized therapies and its successful efforts to broaden its clinical pipeline.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, Vertex carries a debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 0.1x, reflecting a conservative use of borrowed funds. Its current ratio is roughly 2.9x, suggesting a strong ability to meet short-term financial commitments. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was around $3.2 billion, which supports its ongoing investment in research and development.

Johnson & Johnson faces significant legal risks, particularly regarding product liability litigation for its talc-containing products. The company also deals with challenges to its intellectual property rights, as key products like Stelara face potential competition from biosimilars. Additionally, drug pricing reforms in the U.S. and the planned separation of its Orthopedics business introduce operational and strategic uncertainty.

Vertex Pharmaceuticals carries risks related to its high revenue concentration, as nearly all of its sales come from its cystic fibrosis franchise. The competitive landscape for biotechnology remains intense, and the company must navigate pricing pressures from government and commercial payors. Furthermore, the development of cell and gene therapies involves high regulatory uncertainty and significant financial investment in specialized manufacturing.

Johnson & Johnson currently trades at a more modest valuation than Vertex Pharmaceuticals based on its lower multiples for both future earnings and sales.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

The Forward P/E ratio compares a company's current stock price to its earnings estimates for the next twelve months. The P/S ratio measures the market value of the company relative to its sales over the past twelve months.

Johnson & Johnson is an overlooked behemoth compared with faster-growing biotech companies. The business has 28 products and platforms that generate more than $1 billion in annual revenue. Its pharmaceuticals arm, Innovative Medicine, has received two FDA approvals this year and has two more approved drug product launches in the E.U. and the U.S. The Innovative Medicine division accounts for 65% of JNJ's annual revenue and appears to have a robust pipeline beyond the pending products. MedTech, its other arm, sells a wide range of healthcare products, including wound care, surgical instruments and implants, hip and knee replacements, and spinal implants. The recent buy of Atraverse Medical bolsters that business. Revenue for Johnson & Johnson is expected to rise to $101 billion in the current fiscal year. However, Wall Street anticipates a $10 billion drop in net income, to around $16.6 billion.

Vertex Pharmaceuticals continues to benefit from its focus on cystic fibrosis (CF). It recently launched Alyftrek, a once-daily, next-in-class, triple-combination CF regimen. The treatment is seen encouragingly by investors. Alyftrek marks a notable improvement to the twice-daily dosage of Vertex's other CF products and was approved in Australia, New Zealand, Switzerland, the European Union, the U.K., and Canada over the course of 2025, after the U.S. approved it in 2024. Plenty more jurisdictions are evaluating the treatment today. In the U.S., label extensions (the expansion of FDA approval for use) mean Vertex can treat 95% of people with cystic fibrosis in the country today.

Vertex has expanded into treating other conditions. Povetacicept, an investigational recombinant fusion protein therapeutic, continues to show best-in-class potential as a treatment for three chronic autoimmune diseases: IgA nephropathy (IgAN), primary membranous nephropathy (pMN), and generalized myasthenia gravis (gMG). The FDA has granted its Breakthrough Therapy Designation for IgAN, with potential approval by Nov. 30 this year, as well as Fast Track Designation for pMN. If approved across the IgAN, pMN, and gMG indications, peak annual sales could reach $4 billion to $7 billion, according to equity analyst firm Argus.

For fiscal 2026, Vertex sales should rise about 10% to $13.3 billion, with net income coming in roughly even with 2025.

Both of these pharma giants can make a compelling argument for investors' dollars. Johnson & Johnson offers better value, based on its P/E and P/S ratios, and stands as the better buy for 2027.

#2926. 3 Dividend Kings to Buy in November That Could Pay You for the Rest of Your Life

Walmart, Lowe's, and Genuine Parts have raised their dividends annually for more than 50 straight years, and each one is making big moves this month.

This is a big week for two retail chains that tens of millions of Americans walk into regularly without a second thought. Lowe's reports its third-quarter results on Wednesday before the opening of trading, and Walmart follows on Thursday.

Both are Dividend Kings — companies that have raised their dividends every year for at least 50 consecutive years. Not just paid one, but raised it, through recessions, oil shocks, and every ugly market in between. Fewer than 60 companies are currently on that list. Another is Genuine Parts, the company behind NAPA Auto Parts, which I also view as a smart buy this month.

That steadiness is what makes all three worth a look if you want income streams that will likely still be growing decades from now. When a dividend-hiking run gets that long, the annual increases become more than habit — they become a central part of the investment thesis, and no board wants to break the streak. Here's what each of these companies is doing right now to keep theirs going.

Walmart (WMT -0.69%) raised its dividend for the 53rd straight year in February. CFO John David Rainey called the raise "a proof point of our continued confidence in our business performance and forward momentum." What I like more is how it's treating shoppers this fall.

Walmart paid billions in tariffs during the earlier phases of President Donald Trump’s trade wars, and it raised prices to pass them along to customers. But the Supreme Court ruled early in 2026 that those tariffs were illegal, and as a result, Walmart alone got back about $2.9 billion in tariff refunds this year. Instead of pocketing the cash, it has been cutting prices. It had more than 11,000 rollbacks running in the second quarter, up from about 7,200 three months earlier.

"We're investing heavily in price because customers need us to, and because we believe it drives market share gains over time," CEO John Furner said.

That's also the catch for Thursday. Walmart told investors to expect only 2% to 4% operating income growth this quarter because of all those price reductions, and Furner admitted customers are "still feeling some pressure."

The retailer’s holiday push is aimed squarely at stretched budgets. Walmart's holiday meal basket feeds 10 people for $35, with more food than last year's. It's running three sales events between Nov. 12 and Dec. 2, and now bundles Walmart+ and Sam's Club Plus memberships for $120 a year.

Walmart is getting better at helping people shop, too. The number of customers using Sparky, its AI shopping assistant, is up 70% from last year, and they spend 40% more per order than shoppers who skip it. Furner described one shopper asking Sparky for a week of high-protein meals and receiving recipes, with every ingredient added to the cart with one click.

Walmart sells groceries and household basics, the heart of consumer staples, so it doesn't need a strong economy to keep its customers. I'm buying the stock before Thursday.

Lowe's (LOW -1.99%) has paid a dividend every quarter since going public in 1961, and it has raised that payout every year for more than half a century.

This year has been harder than many. Home improvement is a consumer discretionary business, and people may put off building a new patio or renovating a kitchen when gas prices are unusually high.

"Elevated fuel prices combined with broader economic uncertainty have influenced household budgets," CEO Marvin Ellison said in August. At the time, Lowe's said it expected sales at existing stores to be roughly flat this year.

Contractors, online orders, and installation services kept it growing anyway, for a fifth straight quarter. Ellison said that growth came "despite pressure in discretionary DIY spending." The shelves are changing to match. Lowe's is adding more than 150 new DeWalt items and bringing Traeger grills into stores and online nationwide. It also bought two businesses that serve builders and contractors, though high mortgage rates are slowing new home construction, which is hurting the performance of both of those acquired businesses for now.

The retailer is also finding new ways to reach people. Its AI shopping assistant, Mylow, has fielded more than 25 million questions from customers and employees, and online shoppers who use it buy at triple the rate of those who don't.

On Nov. 10, Lowe's became the exclusive home improvement partner of Bilt, a rewards platform with more than 8 million members who earn points on their housing payments.

"Home improvement is personal," said Lowe's Chief Marketing Officer Jen Wilson, and the deal lets Lowe's "meet customers in a community they already know and love." A curated Lowe's marketplace inside Bilt is planned for early 2027.

The DIY slowdown is already built into its forecast, so Wednesday’s results don't need to be great, just steady. I'd buy ahead of it and Lowe's Dec. 9 investor conference.

Genuine Parts (GPC -1.29%) has raised its dividend for 70 straight years. Early next year, it splits into two companies: the NAPA-led auto parts business, which keeps the Genuine Parts name, and Motion, its industrial parts supplier.

Court Carruthers, who will run the auto side, said the split gives it "greater flexibility and focus to successfully compete across our global markets." He also put the business plainly: "The mechanic in the garage turning a wrench. This is the core of who GPC serves and how the business was built." He praised NAPA's independent store owners, too: "They know their markets. They know their customers. They build trusted local relationships."

Behind the counter, NAPA just opened its first heavily automated distribution center in eastern Pennsylvania to get parts to those garages faster.

The weak spot for the company is drivers' wallets.

"Our experience indicates that higher energy prices from the Iran conflict are weakening consumer sentiment," CFO Bert Nappier said. Comparable sales to its retail customers fell 3% last quarter, and the company trimmed its profit forecast for the year.

CEO Will Stengel, who will lead Motion, said the company remains "on track to launch GPC and Motion as two independent, leading companies in the first quarter of 2027." The next quarterly dividend goes out to shareholders on Jan. 5, with an ex-dividend date of Dec. 4.

#2923. Top Wall Street analysts prefer these dividend stocks for boosting portfolio returns

Dividend stocks remain a popular choice for investors seeking steady income and higher portfolio returns. However, with thousands of dividend-paying companies to choose from, identifying the right stocks can be challenging.

In this regard, recommendations from top Wall Street analysts can provide useful insights and help identify dividend stocks backed by solid fundamentals and with attractive upside potential.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Independent oil and natural gas company Permian Resources (PR) is this week's first dividend stock. The company recently paid a quarterly base cash dividend of 16 cents per share. At an annualized dividend of 64 cents per share, PR offers a dividend yield of 3.5%.

Recently, Evercore analyst Chris Baker initiated coverage of Permian Resources stock with a price target of $25. The analyst believes that the company is well positioned to benefit from improving U.S. shale demand after the Iran conflict, thanks to its low-breakeven inventory that can boost free cash flow growth. Baker also noted PR's disciplined consolidation in the Permian Basin.

Furthermore, the 5-star analyst highlighted the company's focus on a single basin and management's efficient capital allocations across expansion efforts, strategic acquisitions, and share buybacks. Baker noted that management focuses investments on the higher-return Northern Delaware Basin, helping boost profitability.

"The key piece of our work here, and the reason we think PR deserves a higher multiple relative to more finite or less flexible shale stories, is that PR runs an acquire and exploit model," said Baker.

He explained that Permian Resources deserves a premium valuation as it continually acquires and develops new high-quality assets instead of relying on a limited inventory, a strategy that is the market is underappreciating.

Baker ranks No. 862 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 75% of the time, delivering an average return of 48.3%. See Permian Resources Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Valero Energy (VLO) is a manufacturer and marketer of petroleum-based and low-carbon liquid transportation fuels and petrochemical products. At a quarterly dividend of $1.20 per share, or annualized dividend of $4.80 per share, VLO stock offers a yield of about 2%.

Heading into Valero's second-quarter earnings on July 30, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on VLO stock and increased the price target to $286 from $283 to reflect updated estimates.

Specifically, the 5-star analyst raised his 2026 and 2027 earnings per share estimates to $31.42 and $23.07 from $29.42 and $21.06, respectively, while leaving the 2028 EPS estimate unchanged at $20.37. Mehta made these revisions based on several factors, including updated commodity price assumptions and changes to refining capture rates.

Despite a strong year-to-date rally in VLO stock, Mehta still finds it compelling due to his more positive refining outlook. Moreover, the analyst sees the possibility of solid estimate revisions, which could drive the stock higher. He believes that Valero is well-positioned to benefit from improving refining market conditions due to its strong position in the Gulf Coast, solid balance sheet strength, and low-cost operations.

"Additionally, we believe the company's premium asset portfolio and crude slate optionality should support capture rates and stronger cash flow generation in the near-term, ultimately supporting shareholder returns," said Mehta.

Mehta ranks No. 742 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 59% of the time, delivering an average return of 10.2%. See Valero Energy Statistics on TipRanks.

Moving on to Ovintiv (OVV), a North American oil and natural gas producer. It has solid positions in North America's premier oil basins – the Permian and the Montney. OVV offers a quarterly dividend of 30 cents per share, or an annualized dividend of $1.20 per share, implying a 2.3% yield.

Following meetings with management, RBC Capital analyst Gregory Pardy reaffirmed a buy rating on Ovintiv stock with a price target of $70, highlighting that the stock is on RBC's Global Energy Best Ideas List.

"In our eyes, the depth of Ovintiv's Montney position, streamlined portfolio, strong balance sheet and enhanced shareholder returns afford investors with an attractive valuation re-rating opportunity over time," said Pardy.

The 5-star analyst stated that his meetings with management bolstered his confidence in the company's outlook and potential to achieve a higher valuation. Pardy noted Ovintiv's transformation, with the company streamlining its portfolio from six basins (including the Uinta, Bakken and Anadarko) to two – the Montney and Permian – while enhancing the depth of its inventory.

Pardy also emphasized OVV's improved shareholder returns and solid balance sheet following the recent sale of its assets in the Anadarko Basin for $3 billion.

The company reduced its nonaccrual exposure by 44% in dollar terms through successful credit workouts and proceeds from repayments. Management successfully accessed the debt markets with a $300 million unsecured bond offering, extending its maturity profile and maintaining leverage at the midpoint of its target range. The portfolio remains centered on senior secured lending, with first-lien debt making up nearly 80% of total investments and a focus on larger, resilient companies with median EBITDA of $180 million.

Operator: Welcome, and thank you for joining Oaktree Specialty Lending Corporation's Fourth Fiscal Quarter 2026 Conference Call. Today's conference is being recorded. [Operator Instructions] I will now turn the call over to Alison Mermey, OCSL's Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Raghav Khanna, Co-Chief Investment Officer, will cover portfolio activity; and Chris McKown, CFO and Treasurer, will close with a review of our financial results before we open the call for questions. Now I'll turn the call over to Matt Pendo, President of OCSL. Matt?

Mathew Pendo: Thank you, Alison, and good morning, everyone. This was down about 120 basis points from a year ago and relatively unchanged from June. In dollar terms, non-accruals at fair value have fallen from $81 million a year ago to $45 million today, a reduction of 44%.

Importantly, nearly 85% of the decline in non-accrual dollars over the past year came from proceeds received and investments returning to accrual status. We believe this reflects our team's ability to successfully work through challenging credits. Raghav will walk through additional updates to non-accrual positions in his remarks. There were several positive developments to our balance sheet this quarter, including an update to our ratings outlook and a bond offering. First, in August, Moody's revised our outlook to stable and kept our Baa3 rating unchanged. Second, in September, we priced $300 million of 5-year unsecured notes due 2031 with a 7% coupon and a spread of 240 basis points over U.S. treasuries.

After swapping the floating rate, the equivalent spread to SOFR is 258 basis points. This was our first bond issuance in over a year, and we were pleased with the outcome in a choppy market backdrop. Demand was strong with a final order book more than 3x the size of the deal and included new OCSL bond investors. We want to thank the fixed income community for their support on this transaction. The incremental cost of the new financing is less than $0.05 per share per quarter. After the January 2027 notes are repaid at maturity using borrowings under our revolving credit facility, we will be left with a well-staggered maturity profile, and our next debt maturity is February 2029.

We maintained conservative leverage during the quarter, ending September 30 at 1.00 net debt to equity. Over the course of fiscal year 2026, we maintain net leverage between 0.97x and 1.07x, well inside the long-term target range of 0.9x to 1.25x. Liquidity was approximately $1.04 billion at quarter end. That figure is temporarily elevated because the January notes have not yet been repaid. Pro forma for that repayment, liquidity is approximately $689 million, in line with last quarter and a year ago. Turning to financial highlights for our fourth fiscal quarter and fiscal year. Adjusted net investment income was $29.6 million or approximately $0.34 per share, down from $32.2 million or $0.37 per share in the prior quarter.

This decrease primarily reflected a lower average portfolio balance and a higher income-based incentive fee. For the full fiscal year, adjusted net investment income was $131.7 million or $1.49 per share compared to $151.3 million or $1.76 per share for the 2025 fiscal year. Now turning to the dividend. Our Board declared a total cash dividend of $0.32 per share for the quarter, composed of a base cash dividend of $0.30 per share and a supplemental dividend of $0.02 per share. The dividends are payable in cash on December 31, 2026, to stockholders of record on December 15, 2026.

As a reminder, we adjusted the base dividend in May to be covered by earnings at our current conservative leverage and maintain the supplemental dividend equal to 50% of adjusted net investment income in excess of the base dividend. Dividends declared in fiscal 2026 totaled $1.39 per share, which represented 108% of adjusted net investment income. As we look to fiscal 2027, our top priorities are unchanged: resolve non-accruals, exit non-income-producing equity positions and redeploy those proceeds into performing assets. With net leverage of 1.00x and nearly $700 million of pro forma liquidity, we have the flexibility to be opportunistic as new investments and strategic opportunities arise.

Armen Panossian: Thank you, Matt. Since this is a fiscal year-end call, I want to compare where we stood a year ago with where we are today. Instead, markets saw increased volatility in early 2026 amid concerns of AI disruption, geopolitical uncertainty and renewed inflation pressures. It's a good reminder of why Oaktree's investment philosophy is tied to fundamental credit analysis rather than macro forecasting.

Fast forward to today, with Brent crude rising above $100 per barrel during the September quarter and large AI-related CapEx adding to inflation pressures, the Fed instead raised rates by 25 basis points. That put the federal funds rate at 3.75% to 4% and the 10-year treasury yield moved above the symbolic 5% threshold, reaching its highest level in nearly 2 decades. A year ago, the debate was how far rates would fall. Today, it is how long they stay high and how high.

Our view is that a move in short-term base rates from approximately 4% to 5% would remain manageable and could be beneficial to investor returns as most of the increase would flow through to net investment income. For OCSL, 91% of our debt investments are floating rate and a higher base rate increases contractual interest income as loans reset. U.S. leveraged loans returned nearly 2%, supported by floating rate coupons that limit sensitivity to rising rates, while high-yield bonds declined by almost 2% as treasury yields rose. Corporate fundamentals remain broadly resilient, but the weakest leverage credit lagged, reflecting increasingly selective investor appetite and the growing strain of elevated borrowing costs. On deal activity, direct lending volume rebounded slightly in September, although year-to-date deal flow and average deal size remained below that of last year.

As the broadly syndicated loan market continued to tighten in the quarter, the premium that direct lending new originations offered over new broadly syndicated loans widened to over 150 basis points. Raghav Khanna: Thank you, Armen. I'll start with new originations and exits, then discuss non-accruals before closing with portfolio metrics. Turning to originations. The transaction refinanced the company's existing debt and supports further expansion, including internationally. The investment was underwritten and structured by our European private debt team that has deep local market knowledge and direct engagement with the management team. We like the company due to its long operating history, hard-to-replicate footprint, high quality of schools and strong revenue visibility. It also operates in an industry with several demand tailwinds that includes statutory funding obligations, a persistent structural supply shortage and high barriers to entry. This deal demonstrates the value of combining on-the-ground presence and regional expertise with global relationships. During the quarter, we also participated in 3 performing equity investments that increased our equity exposure to 5.5% of fair value from 3.9% last quarter.

These income-producing equity deals are highly structured with negotiated downside protection and offer compelling risk-adjusted returns for our portfolio. Moving now to exits and prepayments. Proceeds from prepayments, exits, other paydowns and sales were $198 million compared with $263 million last quarter and $177 million last year. We were repaid in full on several private investments during the quarter. Some borrowers were taken out in the broadly syndicated loan market and some were refinanced by other private lenders. A notable exit in the quarter was the repayment of our first lien term loan in RumbleOn, which appeared in our schedule of investments as RideNow Group, a publicly traded company that operates powersports retail dealerships and an e-commerce business.

We were the agent on the term loan, which originally funded in 2021 to finance RumbleOn's acquisition of the RideNow powersports platform. Integration challenges and weaker post-COVID consumer spending pressured EBITDA and put covenant compliance at risk, leading us to mark the loan down to 94% in the year 2023. Importantly, our highly structured loan prevented value leakage during the company's period of underperformance, and we worked collaboratively with the company on a turnaround plan involving new management, cost reductions, asset sales and capital raises.

These actions reposition the company for growth, and we were willing to provide relief to the company in the form of covenant resets and a maturity extension in exchange for debt paydowns during this time to rightsize the balance sheet. In September, RumbleOn refinanced its term loan and our remaining $35 million position was repaid at 101, including an exit fee, a year ahead of the 2027 maturity. This is another example of how our focused structuring capabilities, patience, collaboration with management teams and discipline yielded a positive outcome for OCSL stakeholders. Turning to non-accruals. At September 30, 6 companies were on nonaccrual, the same as last quarter and down from 10 a year ago.

Non-accruals represented approximately 1.8% of the total debt portfolio at fair value. This also represents 4% of the total debt portfolio at cost, which is down 20 basis points sequentially and 250 basis points from a year ago on a cost basis. One investment came off non-accrual, one new tranche in an existing non-accrual name was added and one new borrower was added. BayMark came off non-accrual following the resolution by lenders to recapitalize and stabilize the business. As a reminder, in December 2025, we placed the second our term loan on non-accrual and marked our equity to 0.

It was a fast-moving court supervised process and in late October, the sale to Teva closed at a value in line with our carrying mark of [ 83 ]. Teva funded $57.5 million upfront at closing with the balance payable upon certain regulatory and commercial thresholds.

We're pleased to say that on November 13, Teva received FDA approval for BioXcel's drug, which has triggered the full $67.5 million additional milestone to the lenders. Weighted average yield on debt investments was 9.4% compared with 9.3% last quarter. The portfolio remains well diversified with 170 portfolio companies. Christopher McKown: Thank you, Raghav. In our fourth fiscal quarter ended September 30, 2026, adjusted total investment income was $68.0 million, down from $69.2 million in the prior quarter. The year-over-year decrease was primarily attributable to lower reference rates and a lower average portfolio balance. The year-over-year decrease was primarily attributable to lower reference rates and a lower average portfolio balance. We delivered adjusted net investment income of $29.6 million or $0.34 per share compared with $32.2 million or $0.37 per share in the prior quarter.

The sequential decline was driven by lower total investment income and a higher income-based or Part 1 incentive fee, partially offset by lower interest and other expenses. With 91% of our debt investments floating rate and 100% of our debt floating or swapped to floating, the net impact is positive, all else equal. Although resets are somewhat staggered across the portfolio, we'll see the majority of the impact in our December quarter earnings with the full effect building from there.

Once fully reset, every 25 basis point increase in base rates adds a little over $0.05 per share per quarter to adjusted net investment income with a little over $0.02 per share annualized. Our liquidity was approximately $1.04 billion, including $45 million of cash and $994 million of undrawn capacity under our credit facilities. Ethan Kaye: Great. And then I guess one more quick one. Raghav Khanna: Yes. Ethan, I can take that. Mathew Pendo: And I think, Ethan, just to follow up. I do think -- and we talked about the call like the progress with BioXcel, I think I still think there's progress we can make on the existing non-accruals.

The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and the Federal Reserve Board today published feedback letters for resolution plans submitted in October 2025. The agencies did not identify any shortcomings or deficiencies in these resolution plan submissions.

Resolution plans, also known as living wills, describe a banking organization's strategy for orderly resolution in the event of material financial distress or failure. The agencies conducted a joint review of the 2025 resolution plan submissions from 15 banking organizations with over $250 billion in assets.

In addition, the agencies determined that the shortcoming previously identified in the 2021 BNP Paribas resolution plan has been satisfactorily addressed.
