#2916. Top Wall Street analysts are confident about these 3 stocks for the long haul

Global stock markets have been under pressure as geopolitical tensions have resurfaced in the Middle East. Moreover, investors remain concerned about the sustainability of AI-driven demand and infrastructure spending.

Nonetheless, those looking for attractive stock picks amid the ongoing volatility can gain key insights by tracking the recommendations of top Wall Street analysts. These experts assign ratings after in-depth analysis of a company's fundamentals, growth opportunities, and risks.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

E-commerce and cloud computing giant Amazon (AMZN) is this week's first pick. Heading into the company's second-quarter earnings, TD Cowen analyst John Blackledge reiterated a buy rating on AMZN stock, citing strength in the Amazon Web Services cloud unit as well as the e-commerce and advertising businesses. The analyst lowered his price target on AMZN stock to $340 from $350 as he revised his estimates and slightly raised his capex projections.

Specifically, Blackledge expects Amazon to report revenue of $200.1 billion, 2% above the Street's consensus, driven by acceleration in AWS and advertising revenue. He also expects the company's e-commerce business to reflect the shifting of Prime Day in the U.S. and other key markets to the second quarter this year, compared with third quarter of last year.

In particular, Blackledge expects AWS revenue to grow 35.5% year-over-year in Q2 2026, marking an acceleration from 28.4% in the prior-year quarter and 3.4% above the Street's expectations. The 5-star analyst expects revenue to be driven by rising generative AI workloads as the company's significant AI infrastructure spending helps to ease supply constraints.

Regarding third-quarter outlook, Blackledge said, "Our rev and Op Income estimates are 0.3% and 3.2% above consensus, driven by further AWS revenue growth acceleration led by AI demand."

Blackledge ranks No. 771 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 55% of the time, delivering an average return of 11.2%. See Amazon Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Moving on to semiconductor company Marvell Technology (MRVL). Following several meetings with management, RBC Capital analyst Srini Pajjuri reiterated a buy rating on MRVL stock with a price target of $360.

"Overall, the meetings reinforced our conviction that MRVL can sustain 40%+ growth for the next 3 years, driven by strong AI demand, optical connectivity leadership, and expanding Custom pipeline," said Pajjuri.

The 5-star analyst added that robust demand and limited supply are giving greater revenue visibility. Pajjuri noted that Marvell's data center business is on track to deliver more than 50% growth this year and next. Also, the growth in the company's networking business is outpacing compute, driven by agentic AI and inferencing workloads.

Meanwhile, Pajjuri noted that optical product lead times have extended to more than six months, while XPU customers are placing purchase orders 12 months in advance. While the analyst kept his estimates unchanged, he sees the possibility of upside for the second half of 2026 from the Optical business, with more significant upside potential for 2027 and 2028 estimates.

Furthermore, Pajjuri noted that Marvell's scale-across offering is emerging as an additional growth catalyst for 2027, while scale-up networking is expected to present a multibillion-dollar greenfield serviceable addressable market. Also, management is upbeat about Marvell's custom business, with the company targeting more than $10 billion in revenue for 2028, driven by existing programs with Amazon's AWS and Microsoft and multiple XPU attach wins.

Pajjuri ranks No. 88 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 75% of the time, delivering an average return of 51.5%. See Marvell Options Activity on TipRanks.

Chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) is scheduled to announce its second-quarter earnings on Aug. 4. Shares have seen a strong jump year-to-date due to demand for the company's AI GPUs and server CPUs.

Ahead of second-quarter earnings, Wells Fargo analyst Aaron Rakers reaffirmed a buy rating on AMD stock and raised his price target to $615 from $505, citing "increasing focus on path to +$20/sh. EPS in CY28." The analyst expects AMD to reiterate its confidence in the MI450 series and Helios ramp beginning in the third quarter of 2026.

The 5-star analyst increased his estimates for AMD server CPU revenue to $16.0 billion (up 68% year-over-year), $20.5 billion (up 28%), and $25.0 billion (up 22%) for 2026, 2027, 2028, respectively. Rakers noted that in the previous quarter, AMD increased its server CPU total addressable market estimates to $120 billion by 2030, representing a more than 35% compound annual growth rate.

Rakers expects AMD to comment on an additional rise in server CPU demand since its first-quarter results. He sees upside driven by agentic AI demand momentum, cloud demand, and traditional enterprise modernization. In this regard, the analyst highlighted that Micron increased its 2026 server shipment guidance recently. Also, checks indicate continued upside to the average selling price.

Meanwhile, Rakers' data center GPU estimates remain above consensus at $15.6 billion, $40.6 billion, and $63.0 billion for 2026, 2027, and 2028, respectively, while estimates for the client and gaming businesses are below the Street's consensus. Overall, the analyst projects EPS of $7.15, $13.40, and $18.75 for 2026, 2027, and 2028, respectively.

#2913. Federal Reserve Board finalizes changes to enhance the transparency and public accountability of its stress test and reduce volatility in its stress test-related capital requirements

An official website of the United States Government

Official websites use .govA .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPSA lock (LockLocked padlock icon) or https:// means you've safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

The Federal Reserve, the central bank of the United States, provides the nation with a safe, flexible, and stable monetary and financial system.

Review of Monetary Policy Strategy, Tools, and Communications

Mergers, Acquisitions, and Other Applications

Financial Stability Coordination & Actions

Financial Market Utilities & Infrastructures

For release at 9:00 a.m. EDT Share

The Federal Reserve Board on Wednesday finalized changes to enhance the transparency and public accountability of its stress test and reduce volatility in its stress test-related capital requirements. The two final rules are largely similar to the proposed rules from 2025. The Board also requested comment on a proposal to better capture differences in banks' business models to generate fee income.

The Board conducts stress tests to ensure that large banks are sufficiently capitalized and able to lend to households and businesses even in a severe recession. In December 2024, the Board announced it would modify the test to improve its resilience.

"The stress test is an essential component of our regulatory capital framework," said Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman. "Today's changes preserve its resilience by ensuring that it is transparent, granular, and risk-sensitive. The public will now have greater assurance that the risks banks take will be reflected appropriately in their stress test losses and their capital requirements."

The first final rule requires the Board to invite public input annually on the stress test scenarios and any material model changes. It also updates the framework that guides the design of the hypothetical scenarios and adopts the models that will be used for the 2027 stress test. In addition, the final rule makes several adjustments to the stress test calendar. The final rule also updates the global market shock component, which is a set of shocks to specific market components applied to banks with large trading books. These banks will now be tested against two global market shock components each year, and the Board will use the shock that produces the largest losses for each firm to calculate the firm's stress test results.

The second final rule requires the Board, when calculating stress capital buffer requirements, to average the results from the two most recent annual supervisory stress tests for firms subject to the stress test in both years. The Board will begin averaging stress capital buffer requirements in 2028 to ensure that only models incorporating public input are used in the calculation.

The proposal would request public comment on a revision to the Board's noninterest income model that would improve the stress test's ability to capture business model diversity across firms. If adopted, these adjustments would replace the current noninterest income model that projects each bank's fee income under stress. Comments are due 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

Together, the changes are likely to reduce year-over-year volatility in capital requirements by approximately 50 percent and are not expected to materially affect aggregate capital requirements.

#2912. Chevron Says AI Has Already Captured Over $100 Million in Value. Here's Where It Might Find an Even Bigger Payoff.

Chevron isn’t a tech company, but it’s already accruing benefits from use of artificial intelligence (AI).

To say that artificial intelligence (AI) stocks are prominent and top of mind for many investors is an understatement. Still, hefty market capitalizations and popularity don't always paint the full picture.

Sure, plenty of companies and high-ranking executives at those corporations are using AI, but many currently struggle to generate tangible profit benefits from the technology. The harsh reality is the vast majority of corporate AI adopters are spending on the technology with little to show for it. Chevron (CVX -0.47%) isn't part of that group.

Chevron is a prime example of a major company benefiting from AI adoption. Image source: Getty Images.

When it reported third-quarter earnings last month, Chevron told analysts and investors it had generated $100 million in year-to-date "operational efficiency gains" backed by AI initiatives. Chevron's AI benefits include a 50% reduction in loss production events in the Denver-Julesburg Basin. Those data points may be signs that Chevron is onto something with its AI ambitions.

No one will mistake Chevron for a technology company, and that's OK. Its primary business is the exploration and production of oil and natural gas, but that makes Chevron (and some of its peers) ideal for broader AI deployment.

Getting down to the heart of the matter, the lifeblood of the energy industry is finding new reserves and efficiently extracting more oil and gas from already tapped basins, offshore deposits, and oilfields. Oil and natural gas prospecting is data- and labor-intensive, time-consuming, and not cheap. AI can improve those scenarios so much that Chevron has its own AI platform, ApEX.

Two interesting facts about ApEX for Chevron investors to consider: First, this is very much an "in-house" product, meaning the oil major is saving some money by not farming out its most important AI needs to a third-party vendor. Second, ApEX was initially tested in deep waters in the Gulf of Mexico. That shows confidence in the platform, as deep-water offshore drilling is often cost-intensive and potentially risky.

Those are points to keep in mind as Chevron looks to solidify long-term earnings growth by probing new fields in locations such as Venezuela while potentially lifting output at domestic oilfields such as the Bakken Shale and the Permian Basin. If there's one thing oil companies love, it's the ability to pull more oil and gas than previously expected from the locations in which they're already operational.

So, in answering "where" in terms of the locations where Chevron can drive AI benefits, the answer could well be "everywhere."

Some industries are struggling with AI adoption, but as Chevron proves, that's not the case in the oil and gas space. Some experts believe one reason for successful AI deployment in the energy sector is that it's a real-world, not a virtual, application.

Beyond that, there's a belief that dedicated energy-sector AI adopters will leverage the technology to improve efficiencies, cut costs, and deliver tangible earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) benefits. And for those worried about the environmental impact of the oil and gas industry, companies such as Chevron can dramatically reduce their carbon footprints by using AI.

The good news is that Chevron is already reaping benefits from AI use, and there's likely more to come in the long term.

#2909. Good News: "Trumpflation" Might Go Away Soon. Here's What This Means for Stocks.

Most of America’s recent inflation came from two presidential policies. But the future of inflation might be brighter in 2027.

A big reason why Donald Trump was reelected as U.S. president in 2024 is that voters wanted him to fix inflation. High costs of living have dogged the U.S. economy since the pandemic, with the inflation rate reaching highs over 9% in 2022.

The Fed has set 2% inflation as its official target. But for the past several years, inflation has been higher than that. The Fed's preferred metric for inflation, the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, has been above target since February 2021 -- almost six years.

Inflation has been a challenge to countries around the world and to U.S. presidents of both parties ever since 2020. The pandemic caused global supply chain disruptions and massive amounts of government borrowing to get through the crisis.

Unfortunately, it seems that Trump's policies in his second term as president have largely made inflation worse. In the recent November midterm election, exit polls indicated that a majority of voters blamed Trump policies for higher prices.

Let's look at why "Trumpflation" might be a big culprit in American consumers' current dissatisfaction about the economy -- and why new Vanguard research shows signs of hope for lower inflation and strong economic growth in 2027.

Trump imposed sweeping new tariffs in 2025 that effectively act as a tax on imports, driving up costs for businesses and consumers. Trump started a war with Iran in February 2026, which has caused global disruptions to the oil market, raising oil prices and driving up costs for household energy bills, gasoline, and diesel fuel. Higher energy costs spill over into the entire economy, driving up prices for airfare, farm fertilizer, food on grocery store shelves, and any consumer goods shipped by truck.

Although these Trump policies have not been severe enough to cause a recession, they have caused a noticeable uptick in inflation. This chart shows what has happened to inflation since Donald Trump took office in January 2025. Look at that big spike after February 2026, when the Iran war started.

US Consumer Price Index YoY data by YCharts

It's possible that inflation might have already "gotten better" -- that America would already have lower inflation in line with the Fed's 2% target -- if not for Donald Trump. According to Motley Fool research, higher energy costs are the biggest factor behind why overall inflation remains so high. Energy inflation was nearly 10 times higher than overall inflation as of September.

But if you want lower inflation, the future is looking more hopeful.

Recent Vanguard research found that inflation is being driven by three major price shocks: tariffs, energy prices, and artificial intelligence (AI) industry demand. Two of those driving forces were caused by Trump's own decisions -- "Trumpflation."

However, Vanguard's analysis has a hopeful message. Tariff effects on inflation are likely to fade soon, as the one-time increase in tariff costs gets “rolled off” from the official year-over-year inflation data. (This doesn't mean the tariffs go away, but the way they are measured will change; the tariff effect on inflation is already built into the economy and will not drive inflation higher.) By April 2027, just from this tariff "roll-off" effect, Vanguard forecasts that core inflation could drop to 2.5%. As of September 2026, the Fed's core inflation rate (PCE price index excluding food and energy) was 3.1%.

What about energy prices? Vanguard's analysis suggests that high energy prices might not subside as quickly, but unless they rise again, their contribution to inflation could be more limited in 2027. Vanguard forecasts a core inflation rate of 2.5% by the end of 2027, with 3% gross domestic product (GDP) growth and only 4.4% unemployment.

There's no guarantee that Vanguard's analysis is correct. However, if you agree that the biggest inflation effects of Trump's tariffs are already "baked in," and that the energy price surge from the Iran war might slowly go away over the next few months to a year, it's reasonable to think that inflation could go lower in 2027.

If both "Trumpflation" policy shocks of tariffs and energy costs go away soon (and Vanguard believes they will), that means inflation might already be closer to the Fed's 2% target. That means fewer Fed rate hikes, lower interest rates, and possibly higher stock prices. The economy could keep growing strong into 2027 and beyond, without getting stuck in "stagflation."

If you're bullish on a future of lower inflation, buying an S&P 500 exchange-traded fund (ETF) is usually a good choice. The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO -1.04%) holds the 500 largest publicly traded stocks in America. The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF has delivered annualized returns of about 12% in the past five years.

If America can get to the other side of the recent spikes in inflation and keep the economy growing strong, this S&P 500 ETF is likely to benefit from that future growth.

#2902. The Nasdaq-100 Is Down More Than 10% From Its High, but the Broad Market Is Down Far Less. Here's How Gaps Like This Have Ended Since 1986.

Twelve past gaps like this one go back to 1986. Did the broad market usually follow tech down?

The broad market, as measured by the S&P 500 (^GSPC -1.03%), has held up much better than tech stocks this fall. The index closed at 7,561.67 on Friday, Nov. 13, just 3% or so under its Oct. 6 record of 7,818.93.

The Nasdaq-100, which leans heavily on big tech and growth stocks, reached its own high close of 31,224.47 the same day. But by Nov. 13, it had fallen to 27,943.74, around 10.5% under the peak.

A gap like this doesn't come along very often. Digging through both indexes' daily closes, I counted 12 past cases since the mid-1980s, plus one in July this year.

But when tech stocks drop this far on their own, does the broad market usually follow them down?

I used Yahoo Finance's daily closes, which don't include dividends, and took each index's best close in the prior 252 trading sessions (around a year) as its high.

A day counted if the Nasdaq-100 closed 10% or more below that level and the S&P 500 closed at most 4% under its own. And so a long slide wouldn't count again and again, a new case needed to start at least six months after the last qualifying day of the one before.

The Nasdaq-100's daily history on Yahoo begins in October 1985, and the first case turned up around a year later, on Oct. 30, 1986.

Most of the others came before 2001, with two in 1997. Three more followed in 2004, 2005, and 2006. After that, the pattern didn't return until March 2021.

This year's case started on July 29. Because the current gap opened on Nov. 2, only about three months later, it doesn't count as a new case by my six-month rule.

Three months after each of the 12 past cases began, the S&P 500 was higher in 11 of them, and the median gain was around 7%. A year later, the index was up again in 11 of the 12, and the median gain came to about 11%. Across every trading day since late 1986, for comparison, it finished the next three months higher around 70% of the time, typically rising about 3%. And it ended the next year higher about 79% of the time, with gains of about 12% at the median.

In other words, the three months after those gaps went better than normal. But the following year looked a lot like an ordinary one.

Most of those gaps closed because the Nasdaq-100 recovered, not because the broader market caught up. In 11 of the 12 cases, it hit a new one-year high within 12 months, after a median wait of 81 days. The July case went the same way, with the Nasdaq-100 setting a new high 55 days later.

Of course, the broad market didn't always stay calm. In six of the 12 cases, the S&P 500 experienced a 10% or greater decline at one point in the following year, including the 1987 crash. Still, it finished the year up in five of the six.

The only case that went badly began on April 3, 2000, a week after the Nasdaq-100's March 27 record close.

Within two weeks, the S&P 500 was more than 10% below its peak. It was down about 2% three months later and roughly 27% a year later. The Nasdaq-100 fell about 66% in that year, and it didn't close above its March 2000 peak again until November 2015.

What set 2000 apart was the run before it. In the previous 252 sessions, the Nasdaq-100 had climbed about 84%, versus about 14% for the S&P 500. As of Nov. 13, both indexes were up about 10% over the last 252 sessions.

Sure, a strong run alone didn't decide things. The Nasdaq-100 had gained about 67% in the year before the February 1999 case, and the S&P 500 still rose about 9% over the next 12 months. But I think today's gap looks much more like the ordinary cases than 2000.

For buy-and-hold investors in an S&P 500 index fund like the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO -1.04%), which closed near $693 on Nov. 13, the history arguably weighs against seeing the gap as a warning. Tech stocks might keep dropping for a while, and this gap may take months to close. But in most of these cases, the broad market didn't follow them down.

I'd consider adding to a fund like VOO now, maybe little by little. Still, 12 cases isn't many, and one was 2000.

#2898. Nvidia Has a $118 Billion Promise Tucked Inside Its Blowout Quarter. Here's What It Means for the Stock

Nvidia crushed expectations again. But its report also shows a growing pile of promises to help customers pay for the data centers that run its chips.

Nvidia (NVDA -0.44%) delivered another huge quarter on Tuesday. Revenue rose 103% from a year earlier to $115.8 billion, and the company forecast $130 billion for the current quarter, according to its earnings release. Shares rose about 5% after hours to around $163.

It was Nvidia's first report since co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO last week. But for long-term investors, one of the most important details sits in the fine print of its CFO commentary.

Nvidia disclosed up to $118 billion in guarantees, meaning it may have to pay third parties "if certain of our partners default on their obligations."

Almost all of that, $105 billion, supports SB Energy's PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in Ohio, which will "exclusively host Nvidia infrastructure under 20-year leases to OpenAI." The remaining $3.5 billion is for neocloud data centers, and $9.5 billion is for power and systems.

Neoclouds are smaller companies that rent out AI computing power. Nvidia also has $32 billion in separate commitments to them, which let it share in their rental revenue.

For scale, $118 billion is more than twice the $53.5 billion in cash and marketable debt securities Nvidia held at the end of the quarter.

Nvidia was direct about the reason. Neoclouds and AI labs "are seeing extraordinary demand for AI infrastructure, yet many are growing faster than their balance sheets and long-term credit profiles can support," it said in the Tuesday filing.

In other words, some customers want more Nvidia computing power than they can finance on their own. By backing the land, power, and buildings, Nvidia helps them raise money, and the chips that fill those buildings come from Nvidia.

The guarantees come with conditions. The Ohio guarantees "take effect phase by phase" as each building is finished, with the first expected in fiscal 2029. Exposure then shrinks over each 20-year lease as OpenAI pays rent. Nvidia said it has not made any payments on its guarantees.

On the earnings call, interim CEO Colette Kress said that if a partner is delayed or runs into trouble before a building is ready, "our guarantee doesn't exist anymore." She added that Nvidia is "rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments and guarantees" as other sources of capital become available.

The same pattern appears on the balance sheet. Accounts receivable, the money customers owe Nvidia, reached $81 billion, more than double the $38.5 billion at the end of January. Nvidia said that this was partly reflected in "extended payment terms on large, multi-quarter agreements with certain investment-grade customers."

None of this changes the core story. Nvidia expects revenue to grow about 75% next fiscal year, and Kress said demand is "far exceeding supply."

But it does change the risk. If AI spending cools, the damage may not stop at slower chip sales. Nvidia could also be on the hook for some of its partners' obligations, and it could take longer to collect what it's owed.

For investors in AI stocks, the guarantee total is worth watching every quarter. If it keeps climbing faster than sales, that could be a sign Nvidia is increasingly paying to create its own demand.

Gabelman ranks No. 554 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 66% of the time, delivering an average return of 14.9%. See Phillips 66 Statistics on TipRanks.

Crescent Energy (CRGY) is an exploration and production company with activities focused in the Eagle Ford, Permian and Uinta Basins. Earlier this month, the company reported better-than-expected Q2 earnings and announced a quarterly dividend of $0.12 per share, payable on August 31. At an annualized dividend of $0.48 per share, CRGY boasts a dividend yield of about 4%.

In reaction to Q2 results, Evercore analyst Stephen Richardson reaffirmed a buy rating on Crescent Energy stock with a price target of $18. He noted continued strength in the company's performance, with second-quarter oil production and cash flow surpassing the Street's expectations.

"CRGY's cash flow exceeded expectations by 10%, reinforcing its trajectory of capital efficiency," said Richardson.

The 5-star analyst highlighted that Crescent raised its full-year oil production guidance, citing the effective integration of the Vital Energy acquisition. Specifically, Crescent tripled its synergy target from the Vital Energy deal to as much as $300 million, significantly reducing the effective purchase price. This reflects Crescent's solid execution following the acquisition, Richardson said.

Additionally, the analyst noted that Crescent's capital spending is and heading toward the lower end of management's prior guidance, indicating disciplined financial controls.

Richardson ranks No. 579 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 65% of the time, delivering an average return of 12.5%. See Crescent Energy Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Finally, Viper Energy (VNOM) is effectively controlled by Diamondback Energy. Viper owns and acquires mineral and royalty interests in oil-weighted basins, mainly the Permian in West Texas. Viper recently announced its Q2 2026 results and declared a 32% hike in its base dividend, effective in the third quarter of 2026. The new base dividend indicates a 4.5% annualized yield.

Viper also removed its quarterly commitment to return at least 75% of cash available for distribution. The company believes that this move will ensure increased flexibility to make opportunistic share repurchases and pursue accretive mergers and acquisitions.

Following the Q2 results, TD Cowen analyst Aaron Bilkoski reiterated a buy rating on Viper, slightly raising his price target to $59 from $58. Bilkoski said Viper's solid Q2 performance supports his view that the strength in oil prices and rising operator activity are driving higher production.

"Viper has delivered, and we forecast will continue to deliver, one of the highest production per share growth profiles in our royalty universe" through the end of 2027, said Bilkoski. He believes Viper deserves a premium valuation, given its above-average growth.

The 5-star analyst said that while the biggest surprise in the quarter was Viper's revision to its shareholder return framework, he doesn't believe that the move indicates a significant change to its underlying strategy. Under the new framework, a larger portion of excess free cash flow is expected to be allocated to share repurchases than to variable dividends, Bilkoski said.

#2872. Spurs' 12-game winning streak: What to know about Victor Wembanyama and the NBA's hottest team

The NBA's hottest team resides in South Texas. After knocking off the Utah Jazz in Salt Lake City on Sunday night, the San Antonio Spurs enter a new week riding a 12-game winning streak — the franchise's longest in more than a decade. Last season featured only two streaks longer than the Spurs' dominant dozen: a 16-game early-season jaunt by the Oklahoma City Thunder (which, as you might remember, these Spurs snapped in the NBA Cup semifinals) and a 13-game run by the Detroit Pistons … who, as luck would have it, will visit the Spurs in San Antonio on Tuesday night.

When a team goes on a winning streak this long, there's plenty of credit to go around. Let's highlight 12 things worth knowing about the Spurs' stampede to the top of the Western Conference — one for each win in the streak! — starting with … I mean, come on, where else can you start?

After the New York Knicks ended his phenomenal third season just short of a championship, Wembanyama entered the summer with a bitter taste in his mouth … and he seems to have entered the new campaign intent on washing it out by devouring everything in his path.

Wembanyama enters Tuesday's action third in the NBA in scoring (a career-high 28.6 points per game) and fifth in rebounding (11.6 caroms a night) while, for the fourth straight season, leading the league in blocked shots (4.3 swats per contest). He hasn't forsaken the 3-point arc, but he's taking a higher share of his shots than ever directly at the rim, and he's converting them at a predictably elite rate, shooting 79.5% in the restricted area — tops among players to take at least 50 point-blank shots.

(Third on that list, by the way? Friggin' Dylan Harper. Don't worry: We'll get back to him.)

Big Vic is averaging — averaging! — 4.64 dunks per game. That's nearly two more flushes per game than last season (2.78), which was already a career high. As tactics go, "Let's get the biggest guy as close to the basket as possible and let him just put the ball into it" seems like a pretty smart strategy, and the Spurs have been reaping the benefits of it, scoring a scorching 126.6 points per 100 non-garbage-time possessions in Wemby's minutes, according to Cleaning the Glass — a mark that would rank head-and-shoulders above the Los Angeles Lakers' league-leading rate of offensive efficiency thus far.

When it comes to "season-opening heaters," most of the attention has gone to the man most responsible for that No. 1-ranked Lakers offense, Luka Dončić — and understandably so. It's worth noting, though, that the big fella is currently on pace to shatter the all-time record for player efficiency rating while leading the NBA in win shares, value over replacement player and total plus-minus; the Spurs have outscored opponents by 257 points in Wemby's 417 minutes, equivalent to a staggering 29.5 points-per-100.

Watch Wembanyama on a nightly basis — not just the "did he just finger-roll from past the free-throw line?!?" highlights, but the possession after possession where he completely warps the opposition's defense and defangs its offense just by standing there — and you come away feeling like the 22-year-old's control of the game is, or at least can be, total.

"Opponents can't really put me in a situation where I can't answer," Wembanyama recently told reporters. "So now all I have to do is not beat myself."

For more than three weeks, he hasn't — and, in a related story, nobody's beaten the Spurs, either.

All right, take it easy there, Thanos. (Not sure if you've heard, but it's all about Dr. Doom right now.)

Generally speaking, if you're in the top 10 on both ends of the floor, you can consider yourself a contender; if you're in the top five on both ends, you're in the inner circle. San Antonio enters Tuesday's action ranked second in the NBA in points scored and allowed per possession, according to Cleaning the Glass.

Where'd the Spurs finish last year, you might ask? Oh, I'm so glad you did. They were … third in points scored per possession, and third in points allowed per possession. If that was good enough to get them to the Finals, maybe bumping up to second both ways will be enough to get them to the top of the mountain this time?

San Antonio has a point differential of +180 for the season — the 21st-highest total ever through the first 14 games of a campaign, according to Stathead. Of the 20 teams above these Spurs, 17 made at least the conference finals; eight of them won it all.

Here's another: The Spurs are blitzing their opponents by 15.2 points per 100 non-garbage-time possessions thus far — the best net rating in the sport. Since the 2003-04 season, only four teams have finished a season outscoring the opposition by more than 12 points-per-100. All four of them — the 2007-08 Boston Celtics, 2014-15 and 2016-17 Golden State Warriors, and the 2024-25 Thunder — went on to win the NBA championship.

According to Jared Dubin's adjusted efficiency metrics at Last Night in Basketball, which measure how much better or worse a team's offense and defense were than the league's average unit in that season, the 2026-27 Spurs currently have a net rating 11.4 points-per-100 better than league average. That ranks third in Dubin's database, which goes all the way back to the ABA-NBA merger in 1976 — behind only Michael Jordan's 1995-96 Chicago Bulls (who won the title) … and this year's Boston Celtics, who (Monday's loss to the Orlando Magic notwithstanding) have been pretty awesome this year.

San Antonio's average margin of victory thus far is 12.86 points per game. Only one team has ever finished a full season higher: the '24-25 Thunder (+12.87) … who, again, won the title.

According to Basketball-Reference's Simple Rating System — a metric "that takes into account average point differential and strength of schedule" — this year's Spurs are 12.75 points better than league average. That's on pace to be the highest SRS rating in Basketball-Reference's database, ahead of teams like the '24-25 Thunder, 1970-71 Milwaukee Bucks, '95-96 Bulls and 1971-72 Los Angeles Lakers — all of whom (say it with me) won the title.

It's early, obviously, and 14 games is too small a sample to draw any definitive conclusions. This much, though, seems clear. If folks start digging into the historical record in search of points of comparison to what you're doing, and they keep coming up with teams that won the NBA championship? You're probably doing something right.

The backcourt logjam that some pundits anticipated last season never really materialized in San Antonio. De'Aaron Fox and Stephon Castle started; rookie Harper mostly came off the bench; the trio shared the floor for just 25 minutes during the regular season and 44 minutes in the playoffs, and the Spurs made it all the way to the NBA Finals. Not actually a problem, right?

Well, that seemed less likely to be the case this season, after Harper authored a breakout performance in his first postseason — and followed it up by making it pretty clear that he wasn't particularly interested in continuing to come off the bench. That led Spurs head coach Mitch Johnson to decide to open this season with all three of his high-octane guards in the starting five, backstopped by Wembanyama with Devin Vassell operating as an ostensible small-ball power forward. The early returns have been explosive:

The Spurs have hammered opponents by 110 points in 141 minutes with Fox, Castle and Harper sharing the floor this season, according to PBP Stats. They're scoring and defending at league-best rates in those minutes … and yes, a lot of that stems from the fact that Wembanyama has been out there for every single one of them. It's also working, though, because the guards are each finding ways to get in where they fit in.

They're flying up the court, with more than 23% of San Antonio's offensive possessions coming in transition in the three-guard lineup, and those units scoring at near-league-best levels on the break. Castle and Harper are almost exclusively taking shots at the rim or from beyond the arc in those minutes, getting to either catch-and-shoot or attack downhill after an initial action bends the defense.

Fox and Castle, both questionable 3-point shooters, have both been knocking down well over 40% of their triples in these alignments. When the pick-your-poison wheel spins to a center guarding Castle, the Spurs have shown their work in developing counters to that scheme.

And while conventional wisdom would warn you against the defensive drawbacks of playing small, with no player listed taller than 6-foot-6 at the 1 through 4 spots, those lineups have rebounded fine, haven't given up a ton of opportunities at the rim, and have yet to be significantly exploited for their lack of size on the perimeter. (It seems that having that French dude back there goes a long way toward bucking conventional wisdom.)

"I understand the narrative around it. I always land on the same reasoning at the very end of it," Johnson told reporters about starting the three guards during the preseason. "They're three of our better players. [...] I think they can dribble, pass, shoot, defend, make winning plays."

Whether they'll continue to do so in this alignment remains to be seen; when offseason signing/veteran power forward Tobias Harris heals up from the calf injury that has cost him the opening month of the season, Johnson will likely have a difficult decision to make. Then again, if the not-so-small-ball Spurs keep blowing everybody's doors off in this look … maybe he won't.

"The biggest thing is, I've got handlers all around me — guys that we want to put the ball in their hands and pick-and-roll around me," Wembanyama said. "That makes things easier."

Since opening the season with losses to the Thunder and Rockets, the Spurs have gotten the opportunity to get right with a pretty friendly stretch of road.

They've had three games against the Jazz, two games against the Kings, and matchups with the Suns and Bulls. They've also caught the Timberwolves without Anthony Edwards or Rudy Gobert, the Mavericks without Cooper Flagg or Kyrie Irving, the Trail Blazers without Ja Morant, and the Warriors right after Stephen Curry went down.

Add it all up, and the Spurs' season-opening slate ranks among the softest in the NBA, according to multiple strength-of-schedule metrics. San Antonio doesn't have to apologize for that, of course. You play the teams that are in front of you, with whoever's in uniform for them when you show up. We've seen plenty of teams fail to capitalize on the opportunity to take down a team at less than full strength. (Looking at you, Mavs.)

Besides, when presented with matchups against shorthanded or sorry opposition, the Spurs have done what good teams are supposed to do: namely, win all of those games, with most of those victories coming by double digits. It's just something to keep an eye on, particularly with a tough opponent like Detroit up next … before three more against the Clippers, Pelicans and Kings. (The games to really keep an eye on? Nov. 27 against Luka and the Lakers, and Nov. 29 against that damn good Celtics team.)

Fox got raked over the coals this summer for his underperformance in the NBA Finals. (Which, it's worth remembering, came with him nursing a high ankle sprain that likely would've sidelined him for weeks had it been the regular season.) His struggles under the brightest lights, combined with Harper's stellar showing in his maiden postseason voyage, primed the pump for the shift to the three-guard lineup, and led to no shortage of calls for the veteran triggerman to cede the stage — and his spot in the Spurs' pecking order — to the rising sophomore.

Well, Fox is still here … and he's kind of threading the needle.

Fox has taken a clear step back in the Spurs' offensive hierarchy, averaging fewer minutes and points per game than he has since his rookie season, and posting far and away the lowest usage rate, time of possession and average number of touches of his 10-year career. He's taking seven fewer field goal attempts per 100 possessions than he did last year.

When Fox shares the floor with Harper and Castle, he's finishing just 15.7% of San Antonio's offensive possessions with a shot attempt, foul drawn or turnover — the kind of usage rate more commonly associated with a complementary player like Isaiah Hartenstein, Toumani Camara or Christian Braun than with a two-time All-Star who has averaged 21 points per game in his career. He's performing well in that reduced role, though.

Fox more frequently takes high-percentage shots — 32% of his attempts are coming at the rim, his highest rate in six years, while corner 3s account for 12% of his shots, a career high — and has almost totally excised long 2-pointers from his repertoire. That, in turn, has led to more efficient scoring. He enters Tuesday's action toting a .551 effective field goal percentage (which accounts for 3-pointers being worth more than 2-pointers) and a .621 true shooting percentage (which factors in 2-point, 3-point and free-throw accuracy) — both of which are by far the highest marks of his career.

He has paired that leaner shot diet with a voracious appetite for freebies, too, drawing shooting fouls on more than 19% of his field-goal attempts — again, a career high. In fact, among 153 players who have logged at least 300 minutes this season, Fox's .496 free-throw attempt rate is the 11th-highest in the NBA, just ahead of free-throw-magnet big men Joel Embiid and Giannis Antetokounmpo.

Pair that just-the-facts-ma'am scoring game with his ongoing facilitation — a team-high 5.8 assists per game, including 33 to Wemby, making them the third-most-frequent assist combo in the NBA thus far — and Fox has managed to continue providing value while still making room for the evolution of the young talent around him. Not bad.

For fans of a certain age, thinking of the Spurs might evoke images of patient, methodical offensive possessions — all entry passes to Tim Duncan on the low block or swing-swing symphonies of "good-to-great" ball movement, where the pace of their play is secondary to the precision of their movements. These aren't your daddy's Spurs, though; these dudes have a predilection toward moving fast and breaking things. Like, for example, you.

In terms of overall pace of play, the Spurs rank just 24th in the NBA, with their average game featuring about 98.8 possessions, according to NBA Advanced Stats. That's due in large part to their defense, though; San Antonio has the longest average defensive possession in the NBA this season, according to PBP Stats. That stands to reason: When you've got to try to figure out how to crowbar open a crevice to attack with Wembanyama menacing along the back line while the likes of Castle and Harper pressure the ball up top, it might take you a little while.

Once the Spurs get the ball, though, they hit the gas. San Antonio has the fifth-fastest average offensive possession this season, and is tied for the fifth-quickest average time to shot, according to Inpredictable.

As noted by the great John Schuhmann, the Spurs lead the NBA in both transition points scored and allowed per game, outscoring opponents by 13 points a night on the break — a massive gap. With their ability to force turnovers, finish possessions with rebounds and advance the ball to all those jet-fueled guards, more than 19% of their offensive possessions come in transition, according to Cleaning the Glass; that's the most in the league. But thanks to their ability to protect the defensive glass, take care of the ball and sprint back, fewer than 12% of their defensive possessions come in transition … which is also No. 1 in the league.

Since at least the start of the 2003-04 season, no team has ever finished the year No. 1 in the league at both generating and preventing transition opportunities. Just another way these Spurs are on pace (ha!) to dispense with conventional wisdom.

Winning the possession battle isn't exactly a revolutionary concept; coaches have been preaching since time immemorial the importance of taking care of the ball on offense and finishing possessions on defense. It's become an increasingly large point of emphasis in recent years, though, as front offices and coaching staffs engaged in the perpetual pursuit of optimization, hunting for every advantage on both ends of the floor. As it turns out, "making sure we get more chances to shoot and score than the other guys" is a pretty solid way to approach things!

The Spurs were pretty good at that last season. When you factor in how many offensive rebounds they pulled in against how many they gave up, how many free-throw attempts they racked up versus how many they conceded, and how many times they turned the ball over compared with how many times they forced opponents to cough it up, San Antonio generated 2.2 more offensive possessions than its opponents per game during the regular season — a good number, but not quite in the upper echelons of the league, like the team that knocked them off in the Finals.

This season, though, the Spurs have tightened the screws virtually across the board. They're grabbing an even higher share of their own missed shots, turning the ball over at the NBA's lowest rate and getting to the free-throw line more frequently, while also forcing more turnovers and curbing their foul rate. Add it up, and through 14 games, San Antonio is generating 7.2 more possessions per game than its opponents — a massive leap over last season, and the No. 1 mark in the league thus far.

Make sure you take more shots on goal than the other guys and you've got a great shot at winning a lot more often than you lose — especially when you put the ball in the hands of dudes who can make those shots. Dudes like …

… the 20-year-old sophomore, whose combination of throwback cool and downhill explosiveness just keeps leaping off the screen pretty much every time you see him.

Harper has responded to his elevation into the starting lineup by continuing to ball out. His usage, free-throw attempt rate and scoring efficiency are all up; his turnover rate is down. Some of that, obviously, comes from more frequently sharing the floor with multiple other high-level ball-handlers, but still: pretty nice to have the guy who's second on your team in touches only coughing it up 8% of the time, one of the lowest rates of any guard in the league.

Coming off that sensational rookie season, Harper is pretty firmly establishing himself as one of the best players in the league when it comes to getting into the paint and finishing on the interior, shooting a frankly bananas 78.6% in the restricted area — better than high-efficiency bigs like Domantas Sabonis, Jarrett Allen, Walker Kessler and Giannis Antetokounmpo. Decent company for a 6-foot-5 sophomore.

Through 14 games, Harper is averaging 18.3 points, 5.5 rebounds, 4.7 assists and 1.0 steals in 31.5 minutes per game, shooting 55% inside the arc, 34% from long distance and 87% from the charity stripe. The list of players to average 18-4-4 for a full season by their age-20 season is just six names long: Magic Johnson, LeBron James, Tyreke Evans, Dončić, LaMelo Ball and Cooper Flagg. Of that group, only Magic shot at least 50% from the field, as Harper is right now.

There's a 7-foot-4 caveat to that, of course. With the exception of rookie Magic playing alongside MVP Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, those other preternatural playmakers didn't have a gravitational force like Wemby pulling attention away from them and opening up opportunities to slash, score and create. But opportunities only matter insofar as you can capitalize on them, and Harper continues to make the most out of his privileged position, perpetually pressuring the defense and looking for all the world like an All-Star in the making — sooner rather than later.

It's not all beer and Skittles in San Antonio, though. As lights-out as the new-look starting lineup has been, moving Harper into the first five has led to some predictable ripple effects in the second unit. The Spurs' reserve corps has a negative net rating for the season, and has — as you might expect — been significantly worse in the minutes when Luke Kornet checks in for Wembanyama, struggling to score even with at least one of Fox, Castle or Harper on the floor.

Some of those struggles might be mitigated by the introduction of Harris, whom the Spurs signed to a two-year, $31 million contract in free agency, and who's yet to play after suffering a left calf strain during training camp. But Johnson will have to shuffle his rotation to make space for the veteran forward. What impact might that have on the minutes and productivity of the likes of Julian Champagnie, whose quick-trigger 3-point shooting has proven so vital for this iteration of the Spurs? Or Keldon Johnson, the reigning Sixth Man of the Year? Or Harrison Barnes, one of just two Spurs (along with Champagnie) knocking down at least 40% of his triples? Or second-year power forward Carter Bryant, whose ongoing development is a clear priority for San Antonio's future plans?

If Harris isn't able to hit the ground running — specifically by spacing the floor at a high level, as he did for Cade Cunningham in Detroit last season — it could throw some sand into the gears of a Spurs offense that has been humming despite not generating a ton from beyond the arc. San Antonio ranks just 26th in the league in the share of its shots that come from beyond the arc, and right around league-average in 3-point shooting accuracy.

That lagging 3-point attempt rate clearly hasn't hampered the offense's effectiveness thus far; some of it stems from the fact that the Spurs hammer the rim as frequently and effectively as nearly any team in the league. After finishing above league-average in 3-point attempt rate the last three seasons, though, you'd imagine Johnson would prefer to find ways to get a few more up — if for no other reason than to be prepared to have multiple styles to play when the postseason comes around and defensive game plans prioritize clogging the paint to take away Wembanyama's rolls to the rim and the three-headed guard monster's driving lanes to the basket.

If opposing defenses are able to congest the interior and force the Spurs to sing for their supper from outside, it'll bring to the forefront perhaps the most significant issue carrying over from last season: whether they have enough bankable 3-point shooting.

As it stands, the entire starting five — Wembanyama, Fox, Castle, Harper and Vassell — currently sits below 35% from deep for the season. Reigning Sixth Man of the Year Johnson is at 22.7%; erstwhile unicorn-turned-indoor cat Kornet hasn't attempted a long ball since April of 2025. The Spurs can make a lot of magic happen in tight confines, thanks to the size and brilliance of Wembanyama, and the speed, skill and force of their guards. If hardly anybody in the rotation can make a jumper when they need to, though, problems will arise.

Those issues — the bench minutes, the shooting, etc. — are not exactly surprises to the Spurs. They're well aware that they've got room to improve.

"If we felt like we're the best version of ourselves at this point in the season, we'll be in trouble," Keldon Johnson recently told reporters.

As excellent as their offense has been, the Spurs have actually underperformed their expected shot quality by the league's fifth-largest amount, according to Synergy Sports Technology's tracking — and all four teams above them in that ranking (Charlotte, Milwaukee, Utah, Chicago) have been terrible, without the talent to meaningfully bridge the gap between expectation and reality. That's certainly not the case in San Antonio.

If Wembanyama (35% from deep last season, 32% this season), Vassell (38% last season, 31% this season) and Johnson (36% last season, 23% this season) tick up toward their previous marks, and any of Fox, Harper or Castle nudge up toward league-average on their looks, this Spurs offense might have another level to reach. Honestly, it might even if only one of those guys keeps the arrow pointed north. You can probably guess which one.

"I can still do more," Wembanyama told reporters after his 52-point masterpiece against the Mavericks. "I mean, my shots weren't falling tonight and that forces me into a style of play that is exhausting. I can do it. I mean, the proof is here. I can do it, but I can be much better if my shots fall. I know it's just a matter of time."

If that happens — if the shots start to fall, the offense soars and the defense remains elite — then it might just be a matter of time before the Spurs are hoisting the Larry O'Brien Championship Trophy, too.

#2871. Ray Dalio says Bessent move is sign that a debt crisis is getting closer; recommends gold and bitcoin

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's debt buyback announcement this week fits into a broader pattern that can signal a forthcoming crisis, according to billionaire investor Ray Dalio.

The Bridgewater Associates founder said Bessent's plan to increase government debt purchases may portend trouble for the U.S. economy. Coupled with the Japanese government reducing its U.S. bond market exposure and surging long-dated American bond yields, Dalio said investors may want to prepare their portfolios for increased risk by owning cryptocurrencies and gold.

"I am confident that the government's financial condition is at an inflection point," Dalio wrote in a LinkedIn post published Friday. "If this is not dealt with now, the debts will build up to levels where they can't be managed without great trauma."

Dalio noted that the Treasury Department has "only limited capacity" to buy back bonds. Bessent told CNBC on Thursday that his team was going to "make a market" and that the purchases would likely top $4 billion.

The U.S. is spending about 40% more than it's bringing in, resulting in the burgeoning budget deficit, Dalio said. The U.S. budget deficit topped $432 billion in July, but Bessent told CNBC that it's likely peaked under President Donald Trump's administration.

Bessent said in the interview that a team was looking at ways to shrink spending by hundreds of billions of dollars. But Dalio said there is "very little ability" to do so given that it is either committed or considered essential.

After years of overspending, Dalio said total debt now dwarfs what the U.S. brings in each year. If the U.S. government was a business, Dalio said debt service payments would come in at roughly $11 trillion — about 200% of annual revenue.

Dalio, 77, warned the cost of repaying principal and servicing the debt will only grow over time.

To solve this, Dalio said the U.S. needs to carefully employ a three-part strategy to get the budget deficit down to 3% of gross domestic product.

First, Dalio said the U.S. government needs to reduce its spending. Second, he said tax revenue needs to be raised. Finally, the New York native and Harvard Business School alumni said lower interest rates were needed.

"All three need to happen concurrently so as to prevent any one from being too large," Dalio said. "If any one is too large, the adjustment will be traumatic."

Dalio cautioned against ramming through these adjustments by "force." For instance, "it would be very bad if the Federal Reserve unnaturally forced interest rates down," he said.

Dalio said it's important to to take steps now, while the economy is healthy. An economy in recession requires increased government spending, he said.

Dalio said the exact timing of a debt crisis can be swayed by variables ranging from military conflict to political change. On its current trajectory, the U.S. could enter such a crisis in as early as one year or as late as five. "My guess, which I suppose will be a bad one, is that it will come in three years, give or take two, if the course we're on is not changed."

To prepare, Dalio recommended investors are underweight debt assets, such as bonds.

As much as 10% to 15% of a portfolio could land in gold, as well as "a bit" of bitcoin, the hedge fund founder said.

Dalio's post came at the tail end of a volatile week for U.S. financial markets. Rising long-term Treasury yields have pressured stocks, leading the S&P 500 to snap a a three-week-long advance.

#2864. It’s becoming increasingly clear why LeBron James signed with the Sixers

When LeBron James chose to sign with the Sixers this past offseason, jaws largely dropped around the league.

He chose the Sixers over a final homecoming in Cleveland? Over a reunion in Miami where he could team up with Giannis Antetokounmpo, Bam Adebayo and Simone Fontecchio?! Over a Bay Area team-up with Stephen Curry and Draymond Green? Over joining Anthony Edwards and LaMelo Ball on the Timberwolves?

Fifteen games into the season, the Sixers now sit atop the East at 12-3. They have the second-best record in the NBA, trailing only the San Antonio Spurs and Los Angeles Lakers, both of whom are 12-2. It's by far the best start LeBron has ever gotten off to with a new team.

And they're doing that with less scoring than ever by The King.

Prior to this year, LeBron had never averaged fewer than 20.9 points per game across an entire season. Through 11 games, he's averaging only 15.1 points while shooting 44.3 percent overall (his worst mark since his rookie campaign) and a career-low 22.5 percent from deep.

On Monday, ESPN's Dave McMenamin reported that "James has asked coaches to be patient with him as he expects to find his rhythm and get his conditioning in line by December as he ramps up." (LeBron quickly denied that on Instagram.) While social media naturally ran wild with that excerpt, what came next was arguably more telling.

"One Western Conference executive told ESPN that James' dip in production is evidence that he knew what he was doing when he picked Philly in free agency in July," McMenamin wrote.

That's what got lost in the debates over LeBron's best landing spots over the summer. Everyone seemingly assumed that he wanted to continue averaging 25-plus points per game while being an offensive focal point of his team. But while LeBron has done a remarkably admirable job fending off Father Time, the man turns 42 in December. And Father Time does remain undefeated in sports, even if he occasionally takes longer than expected to claim his victims.

Last year, the Lakers hit their late-season stride when LeBron shifted into more of a tertiary role. In mid-March, Lakers head coach J.J. Redick outright said "the best thing for our team is [LeBron] being the third-highest-used player." And after the season, LeBron expressed appreciation for how he embraced that new challenge.

"I was put into some positions I never played in my career … actually, in my life," he told reporters. "I've never been a third option in my life. So, to be able to thrive in that role for that period of time and then have to step back into the role that I've been accustomed with over my career … and being able to thrive … that was pretty cool for me at this stage in my career."

Granted, with Luka Dončić and Austin Reaves sidelined in last year's playoffs, LeBron showed against the Houston Rockets that he's still able to conjure his usual magic at times. There will inevitably be games this year where the Sixers ask him to take on more of a leading role, too. Their NBA Cup win over the New York Knicks was a good example of that.

But aside from Tyrese Maxey's megawatt smile luring him in, LeBron might have chosen to sign with the Sixers specifically because he didn't want to shoulder the load every night anymore.

In Miami, he would have been teaming up with a nightly 30-point threat in Giannis. But Bam isn't exactly a world-beater on offense, and the Heat didn't have much in the way of reliable offensive depth behind those two. LeBron likely would have been their second-best offensive weapon most nights, and the floor spacing with him, Giannis and Bam all on the floor together would have been even more clunky than the Sixers' starting five.

The same goes in Cleveland, where Donovan Mitchell would have been the clear lead banana had LeBron signed there. But James Harden has long been most effective with the ball in his hands and a relative non-factor off the ball. Evan Mobley still hasn't taken the offensive leap that he was expected to take a few years ago at this point, while Jarrett Allen isn't much of a threat outside of the paint. At worst, LeBron would have been the Cavs' third-best offensive weapon.

While LeBron is the NBA's all-time leading scorer, he's always been more of a playmaker at heart. Philly gave him the best chance to tap into that part of his game, as Maxey, Jaylen Brown, Joel Embiid and VJ Edgecombe all have the potential to take over and bury an opponent. Throw in shooters like Anfernee Simons and Dean Wade off the bench, and he might have been willing to overlook their flimsy frontcourt depth for the time being.

LeBron's shooting percentages figure to regress positively to the mean as the season wears on, but it's also possible that all of those years of being a runaway freight train to the rim have finally taken their toll. He isn't finishing at the basket as explosively as he has for the grand majority of his career. While that might have been a death knell on another team, the Sixers have the high-end talent to make up for it.

So, yes, LeBron might not have had the same type of emotional attachment to Philly than he did to Cleveland or Miami this summer. But from a pure basketball perspective—especially factoring in his potentially diminished scoring prowess at this age—it's becoming increasingly difficult to argue that he made the wrong choice.

#2860. Top Wall Street analysts believe in the growth potential of these 3 stocks

Geopolitical uncertainty in the Middle East and soaring bond yields weighed on global markets this past week. And investors are closely assessing the valuations of artificial intelligence stocks amid concerns about the sustainability of high spending on AI infrastructure.

Despite those continued challenges, top Wall Street analysts are bullish on the prospects of several stocks due to their long-run growth potential and exposure to lucrative business lines, including AI.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Cybersecurity company CrowdStrike Holdings (CRWD) is this week's first stock pick. The company is scheduled to announce fiscal second-quarter results on August 26.

Ahead of Q2 FY27 earnings, Truist analyst Junaid Siddiqui reiterated a buy rating on CrowdStrike stock and raised his price target to $245 from $187.50. Following CrowdStrike's impressive fiscal first-quarter performance and guidance raise, Siddiqui expects another strong quarter.

The 5-star analyst's optimism is backed by continued strength in Falcon Flex adoption and encouraging large deal activity. Siddiqui also cited continued momentum across emerging products. With the FY27 outlook assuming persistent strength in CrowdStrike's net new annual recurring revenue (ARR), Siddiqui is more focused on the longevity of key growth catalysts such as Falcon Flex adoption, platform consolidation and AI-led demand.

The analyst highlighted that talks with partners were encouraging, with pipeline generation and momentum in large deals remaining healthy in the fiscal second quarter despite tough, year-over-year comparisons.

"We continue to view CrowdStrike as one of the primary beneficiaries of platform consolidation, though we expect investors to remain focused on competitive dynamics and whether current growth levels represent a new baseline or a period of demand acceleration," the analyst said.

Siddiqui ranks No. 226 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 80% of the time, delivering an average return of about 40%. See CrowdStrike Financials on TipRanks.

Shares of personal computer maker Dell Technologies (DELL) have rallied 251% this year, driven by strong demand for AI servers. Recently, Evercore analyst Amit Daryanani reiterated a buy rating on DELL and raised his price target to $550 from $500.

The 5-star analyst contends that while Dell's AI compute segment is getting investors' attention, the company's Storage business is underappreciated and well-positioned to drive revenue and profit acceleration. Daryanani expects the storage business to see higher demand once enterprises start to bring workload back on-premises.

The analyst highlighted that Dell's Storage business, estimated to account for only 10% of FY27 revenue, is one of the factors that could help improve profit margins, given its higher profitability compared to AI servers. Daryanani estimates that the Storage business's operating margin is currently in the low-20% range, while margins for the AI server and traditional server businesses are in the mid-single-digit and mid-teens range, respectively.

Overall, Daryanani views the Storage business as an important catalyst for three reasons: Dell has one of the broadest storage portfolios in the industry; Storage has a significantly higher margin profile than AI servers; and the shift toward proprietary, software-defined storage and AI-focused platforms.

"We think DELL's storage business is becoming increasingly strategic as AI infrastructure deployments move beyond GPU procurement and toward full stack + AI-ready architectures," said Daryanani.

Daryanani ranks No. 19 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 71% of the time, delivering an average return of 38.70%. See Dell Technologies Statistics on TipRanks.

SanDisk (SNDK) is benefiting from AI-driven demand for its memory and storage products. Following the company's 2026 Investor Day event, J.P. Morgan analyst Harlan Sur resumed research coverage of SNDK with a buy rating (it was earlier, "Not Rated") and a price target of $2,250.

The 5-star analyst believes SanDisk is well-positioned to capitalize on a structural inflection reached in NAND demand, driven by strong growth in AI inference. Sur's bullishness is based on three key factors.

First, Sur believes that SanDisk's New Business Model (NBM) framework (or long-term agreements) has enhanced its margin profile and reduced cyclicality. SNDK's eight signed NBMs represent a total contract value of $94 billion and a gross margin of about 80%, even at the floor pricing.

Second, Sur highlighted the growing NAND market and expects the total addressable market to surge from about $70 billion in calendar year 2025 to over $300 billion in 2026 and about $500 billion in 2027. Importantly, the analyst noted that data centers are the largest driver of NAND growth, as hyperscalers increasingly deploy flash for AI inference workloads.

Finally, Sur is optimistic on SanDisk due to its technology dominance. The company's BiCS10 technology is sampling ahead of schedule and has 65% more bits per wafer than BiCS8, the analyst said. Also, Sur expects SanDisk's High Bandwidth Flash to become a differentiated memory platform for AI inference.

"Layered on top, mgmt's commitment to returning 100% of excess cash flow to shareholders should drive an aggressive share count reduction trajectory that further amplifies EPS growth on a per-share basis," said Sur.

Sur ranks No. 15 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 71% of the time, delivering an average return of 43.20%. See SanDisk Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

#2856. Kings are 1-12 and coaching rumors have begun. Two familiar names are surfacing.

The Sacramento Kings are off to a 1-12 start that has started heating up the coach's rumor mill.

The Kings are led by second-year head coach Doug Christie, who took over the position in December 2024 after Sacramento fired Mike Brown. After Christie lead Sacramento to a 27-24 record, the Kings removed the interim tag in April 2025.

Since then, Christie has a 23-72 record, leading to speculation of an eventual coaching change.

According to NBA insider Marc Stein, there are already rumbles in league coaching circles that have named both Tom Thibodeau and Mark Jackson as "potential down-the-road" head coaching candidates for the Kings, if Sacramento eventually makes a coaching change.

More: Kings head coach Doug Christie gets brutally honest about job security

Both candidates would be intriguing, however, the Kings have indicated they have no plans to move on, as they are hesitant to fire Christie, according to The Athletic's Sam Amick.

Thibodeau is a two-time NBA Coach of the Year in 2011 and 2021 and is known for coaching defensive-focused teams that had perennial regular-season success and playoff appearances with the Chicago Bulls, Minnesota Timberwolves and New York Knicks. The Kings have a dynamic point guard in Darius Acuff Jr. and Thibodeau is no stranger to talented point guards having coached Derrick Rose and Jalen Brunson.

Jackson coached the Golden State Warriors for three seasons from 2011 to 2014. He hasn't coached since but has often been credited with helping build the foundation of the future Warriors dynasty led by Stephen Curry, Klay Thompson and Draymond Green. When the Warriors were an afterthought in the league, Jackson's coaching, eye for talent and how to maximize it helped the Warriors become a playoff team before they ascended into a championship team under Steve Kerr.

Christie addressed hot seat rumors after the Kings' Nov. 13 loss to the Portland Trail Blazers.

"I think this seat is hot always, so it doesn't really matter," Christie told USA TODAY. "Obviously, we want to win games. Nobody wants to win more than me, from the standpoint that the record doesn't go on the player's numbers. The record goes on coach's number."

Christie is in the final year of a guaranteed contract. He signed a three-year deal for approximately $2 million a year with the final year (2027-28) a team option.

Sacramento is Christie's first position as a head coach in the NBA. He was the Kings' assistant coach from 2021 to 2024, including the original "Beam Team" that ended a 16-year playoff drought in 2023.

Christie played for seven teams in a 15-season NBA career, including as a starter and defensive enforcer with the Kings during their best era in the early 2000s. Christie made the NBA All-Defensive First Team once and the NBA All-Defensive Second Team three times during his Kings tenure between 2000 and 2005.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Kings are 1-12 and coaching rumors have begun. Two familiar names are surfacing.

#2853. Ukraine damages Putin’s prized Crimea bridge as Zelenskyy lauds ‘unprecedented operation’

Ukraine has damaged the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to the occupied Crimean Peninsula, delivering a symbolic blow to President Vladimir Putin as Kyiv reels from strikes on its own infrastructure.

Sergey Aksyonov, the Russia-installed governor of Crimea, confirmed that the strategically important bridge, which had been briefly closed on Monday, was attacked overnight for the second time in two days.

Videos and photos circulating on social media appeared to show the partial destruction of the bridge, with one section having collapsed into the water. CNBC was unable to independently verify the footage.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the attack as an "unprecedented operation" several weeks in the making, with Ukraine's defense forces, security services and weapons manufacturers involved.

"Russia strikes our infrastructure every day, including bridges in Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro, Kyiv, and the Odesa region," Zelenskyy said Tuesday on X.

"We are restoring our infrastructure. But we are also reminding Russia that war will always return to where it began. Ukraine's defensive capabilities are strong and will remain so, and we will never leave terror against our cities and people unanswered," he added.

Train and vehicle traffic was suspended due to the attack. No injuries have been reported.

Ukraine has repeatedly targeted the bridge since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in early 2022.

A 12-mile crossing of road and railways, the Kerch Bridge is one of Putin's signature projects. The crossing, sometimes referred to as the Crimean bridge, was built on his orders shortly after the Kremlin forcibly annexed Crimea in 2014 to support Moscow's claims to the territory.

Rail traffic on the bridge was opened on one track, Russia's Ministry of Transport said in a statement via Telegram on Tuesday, while restoration work continues on the second section.

The co-owner and chief engineer of Ukrainian missile and drone maker Fire Point, Denys Shtilierman, appeared to confirm the company's role in the attack, following reports that a Ukrainian Flamingo cruise missile was used in the strike.

"We dedicate this to the memory of our friends and colleagues Andriy and Yuriy, without whom this would not have been possible. R.I.P.," Shtilierman said via X on Tuesday. A spokesperson at Fire Point separately confirmed the company's role in the attack.

Analysts at the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, said Ukraine's attacks on the Kerch Bridge were likely part of Kyiv's ongoing and systematic strike campaign aimed at denying Russian forces the use of major ground lines of communication via Crimea.

Russian forces, meanwhile, struck two bridges crossing the Dnipro River in Kyiv.

Vitaliy Klitschko, the mayor of Ukraine's capital, said via Telegram on Tuesday that specialists were working to assess the extent of the damage to the North and South bridges.

Klitschko said Russian attacks on Kyiv overnight had also caused disruptions to water and heating supplies.

The strikes come ahead of Putin's trip to China this week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen, where a trilateral meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping is planned on Thursday.

Asked whether Ukraine's latest attacks might be connected to the upcoming trilateral summit, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said this could not be ruled out.

"Combat operations continue, and our military is striking targets that are somehow connected to Ukraine's military-industrial complex. And Ukraine is continuing its terrorist attacks," Peskov said, according to Russian state news outlet Ria Novosti.
